body: There's a long road in the Florida Panhandle that runs through the river bottoms and crosses the Escambia River, and back around 2004 there wasn't a single streetlight on it. Thick woods on both sides, wildlife management land, nothing out there but the animals.

It's two thirty in the morning, and a twenty-year-old kid is driving west toward the bridge when he sees a shape at the side of the road up ahead. He figures it's about to dart out in front of him, so he stops about a hundred feet short and waits.

It comes out on all fours, angling across the road into his headlights, and the further it comes the bigger it gets. He grew up out there, he knows what a black bear looks like, and this is way bigger than any bear. It's the wrong colour too, a dingy, dirty grey, and nothing that lives in those woods is that colour.
When it reaches the far side of the road, right off his passenger side, it stops. And then it stands up.
On its back legs it's seven feet tall at least, well over five hundred pounds, and its eyes are glowing orange and yellow in his headlights. It doesn't run. It just stands there looking at him.
He said the fear that hit him came from somewhere way down deep, and he knew without any doubt that if it decided to come for him, he wouldn't stand a chance.
Then it turns, steps into the trees, and it's gone.

He floored it out of there and didn't tell a soul for years. When he finally went looking for anything that matched what he saw on that road, there was only one thing that did. People call it the Dogman.

It's July, deep in the redwoods of northern California, and a young couple is spending their first night ever in a tent at Albee Creek Campground. They've brought their two little dogs, a pair of chihuahua-beagle brothers who bark at absolutely everything back home, every cat, every squirrel, every person who walks past the yard. Right behind the tent there's an old stump about three feet high, left from a tree somebody cut down a long time ago, and the wife leaned on it that evening while they cooked steaks over the fire. There was nothing on it.
They lock every scrap of food in the bear box, zip themselves in, and the dogs curl up on their little beds between the sleeping bags.
Somewhere around two or three in the morning, the wife gives her spouse a hard nudge and whispers that something is touching her.

Her spouse rolls over, and in the bit of moonlight coming through the nylon there it is, something pressing in against the tent wall right where her head is, six or ten inches off the ground. And then it pulls back, like it heard them.
She wants to go out and look. Her spouse says absolutely not, stay still, stay quiet, and she inches away from the wall.
And those two dogs, the ones that bark at everything, don't make a single sound. They're shivering hard and trying to burrow down into her sleeping bag between her legs.
After a while they hear it moving off, slowly, through the leaves. No growl, no smell, nothing else at all.

Nobody sleeps the rest of that night. And in the morning, on top of that old stump behind the tent, the one that was bare the night before, there's a little pile of small, smooth, polished stones, the kind you'd pick up out of a riverbed.

When they hand in their pass they ask the ranger what animals are around. A few deer, he says, some elk, raccoons and foxes, and he hasn't seen a bear near Albee in a year or two. So would any of those come up and push on somebody's head through a tent wall?
The ranger just smiles, and shrugs, and doesn't say a word.

Durham, North Carolina, May 2019. An ordinary two-storey house in an ordinary subdivision, and the rest of the family is away for the night, so one guy is home alone with the dog. She's been acting anxious lately, anxious enough that they just took her to the vet about it.

Around half past midnight he takes her out back on her long leash. He's in his socks and doesn't want to step in the wet grass, so he stays at the back door of the garage while she wanders into the narrow strip between her kennel and the house. There's one dim light on the garage wall and that's it. She's facing him, doing her business.
And then her back end lifts up into the air, a foot, maybe two, like something behind her has grabbed hold and pulled.

He screams. She tears herself loose and bolts back to him, and in the dark behind her he hears something moving over the rocks along the wall. Then it steps forward, right to the edge of the light, and stops.

It's tall. He's six foot two and he has to look up to where he thinks its head is. It's pale, not white, just the pale skin of somebody who hasn't been outside in a couple of weeks, and it's long and lanky and put together wrong somehow.
It looks at him for a second, maybe two.
Then it goes backwards into the dark, faster than he could ever move, and it's gone.
Half an hour later the police knock, probably called by a neighbour who heard him screaming. He tells them he saw a man in the backyard. He couldn't make himself tell them the rest.
He doesn't believe in this stuff, and some days he tells himself it was just a really tall guy on drugs. But he hasn't taken that dog out alone since.

It's one in the morning on Thanksgiving, and a car is doing fifty-five down Highway 18 in Oregon, through nothing but dark hay fields. There's a grandparent in the passenger seat and a grown son at the wheel, and they're racing to a children's hospital in Portland, because the baby swallowed a pill at the beach house that night and the ambulance has already gone on ahead. Nobody's talking. The son is so tired he keeps drifting over the line, so the grandparent is wide awake, watching him and watching the road.
Way down the highway, right in their lane, something is running toward them.
At first they both figure it's a deer. Then it gets closer and they can see it's a horse, a golden horse galloping straight down the middle of the road at them in the dark, and it's coming fast.

About a hundred and fifty feet out, it jumps. And somewhere in the air it stops being a horse and turns into an owl, a giant owl, with wings so wide they stick out past the edge of the lane, twelve, maybe fifteen feet across. The son swears and yanks the wheel, and the thing comes down on the shoulder just ahead of them on the right.

As they go past, it doesn't fly away. It just tucks its head down and pulls its wings in tight against its chest like it's hiding, like it's scared of them. The grandparent looks right at it through the window, and even folded up like that it comes up to the bottom of the glass, three and a half feet of owl sitting on the side of the highway.

Here's the part that gets me. Neither of them said a word about it, not one, for the rest of the drive. A strange calm just came down over the both of them, the son wasn't sleepy anymore, and they drove all the way to Portland in total silence like nothing had happened.

It wasn't until the next afternoon, driving home past that same stretch of road, that it all came pouring out of them at once, and they'd both seen exactly the same thing. (The baby was fine, by the way.)
They still think it was something good, something watching over them on the worst night of the trip. Or maybe it was something they were never supposed to see.
Fall of 2010, just after dark, two roommates are driving south on the I-5 in southern Oregon, climbing the long steep grade up Sexton Mountain Pass toward Grants Pass.

Near the top, the driver notices two bright white lights hanging over the hill. As they climb, a third comes into view, and then a fourth in the middle, amber, blinking slowly. The three white ones make a triangle, it's huge, and it isn't moving at all.
They talk about it the whole way up and agree it's no plane. And then the highway carries them right underneath it.

The roommate sticks his head out the window and looks straight up, and he can just make out the shape, a dark triangle with a light at every corner. It takes so long to drive under that the driver figures it was about as wide as a football field, and it doesn't make a sound.

Here's what still bothers the driver. Those lights were blinding, and the amber one was right over their heads, but they didn't light up the road or the trees or anything at all. Lights that bright should've lit up the whole mountain.
Over the crest it seems to drift back the way they came, and then the hill hides it.

That should've been the end of it. But more than ten years later the two of them got talking about that night, and their stories don't match. The driver remembers pulling over to roll the windows down and listen, then driving on and watching it shrink in the mirror. The roommate remembers stopping right under it and climbing out to dig the camera out of the back, and when they looked up, it was gone.
The driver filed a report a couple of days after, and when they dug it up it matched the driver's version. So one of them is remembering it wrong, and the driver would rather leave it at that.

Except for one more thing. When they got to the driver's parents' house an hour later, bursting to tell them, the parents, who were always night owls, just seemed strangely tired, and went straight to bed.
This one doesn't happen in the woods. It happens in a supermarket, in broad daylight.

Two sisters, ten and eight, are at the Ralphs near home in Southern California while their mom waits at the pharmacy counter, so they're doing what bored kids do, racing each other up and down the aisles and giggling.

The older one comes speed-walking around the end of an aisle and nearly runs straight into a boy. He's maybe ten or eleven, tall for his age, blond, plain clothes, a totally blank face, and his eyes are solid black, edge to edge, with no white in them at all.
And he smiles at her, just a little, like her being scared is funny to him.

Both girls freeze. Behind the boy there's a younger girl, maybe seven, short blond hair, standing with her back to them. Then, like she can feel them there, she turns around, and her face is just as blank, and her eyes are the same solid black.

The older sister grabs the younger one and runs as fast as she can, aisles away, and when they finally stop they look at each other and burst out laughing, the way you do when you can't believe what just happened.
Later they bring their little sister back to see. The two kids are gone.

She's the first to admit they'd just been reading about black-eyed children online, so maybe that put the idea in their heads, and maybe those two were just a brother and sister with some kind of eye condition.
But she wasn't the only one who saw them. Her sister was right there, and all these years later she remembers it exactly the same way.

Summer of 1998, in the hill country between Mount Rainier and Mount Adams, and a seventeen-year-old kid finally gets his turn at his uncle's cabin near Randle, Washington, three quarters of a mile up a twisting gravel road with nothing behind it but forest.

It's about a quarter to eight on the second evening and they're driving back up from fishing when they both see something moving fast through the alders by the cabin. It's upright, it's big, and it moves like a house spider, way quicker than anything that size has any right to. His uncle stops the truck, figuring it's a prowler.

The figure stops in the trees with its back to them and starts to sway, and in the shade it almost disappears. So his uncle rolls the truck forward until they're about ten yards off, and it comes out, seems to realize it's cornered, and squats down, dropping something it's been carrying.

Standing, it'd be a bit over six and a half feet, lean and muscular and broad through the chest, with blackish grey fur flecked with brown. The skin of its face is dark and wrinkled like an elephant's, and the head is small for the body.

And it looks terrified. Its lower jaw is sticking out and its lips are quivering, and it's picking nervously at the gravel and rocking its upper body in little circles, the way an owl does. He has a strong feeling they're looking at a youngster.

For about ten seconds nobody moves. Then he reaches, very slowly, for the Polaroid in the console, and the second he opens the truck door, gravel comes rattling off the windshield and off him, and the thing crashes away into the brush.

The photos came out blurry. But what it dropped was a flattened, dried-out garter snake about a foot and a half long, and the air smelled like singed hair and wet dog and really strong body odour. His uncle, a dry, no-nonsense guy, just said, 'Welp, you don't see that every day, do ya?' and then he'd only talk about fishing.

Around half past ten that night his uncle steps out on the deck for a smoke, and maybe fifty yards down in the ravine something big is crashing through the brush. With it come deep, chesty shouts, and one deep voice keeps starting the same phrase over and over, and every time it breaks off into a long, booming 'baaa-woop'.
His uncle just joked that the young one was getting an earful.

Central Kentucky, a summer night in 2006. A guy in his early twenties has been poking around the big old farm next to where he grew up, and he's lost track of time, and now it's dark. There's a full moon though, bright enough to see by.
He's standing between two tobacco barns near the farm road when something big comes bursting out of the dark on his right.

It shoots past him in a blur, right past him, and disappears around the corner of one of the barns. It's so fast his first thought is that somebody's cow got loose. Except it seemed way too tall to be a cow.
So he takes a few steps toward that corner to see.
He never gets there. Before he does, the thing steps sideways back into view, standing upright, facing him, maybe ten feet away, and he freezes.

It's about six foot four and grey, with a long snout and tall, pointed ears. One arm is resting up against the barn wall like it's just leaning there, casual, watching him. There seem to be dark rings around its eyes and its mouth, but the moon leaves a lot of it in shadow. It has a tail, not a big one.
And the eyes. That's what he remembers most, a hard, fierce stare, locked right on him. It doesn't make a sound.
Five seconds of that, maybe. Then he turns and runs harder than he's ever run in his life, and he doesn't stop for half a mile.
He's told hardly anybody, because he figured they'd laugh. But almost twenty years later he still can't shake it, the grey fur, and how fast it was, and one question he keeps coming back to.
It ran right past him, close enough to touch, and then it came back and just stood there and looked at him. So why didn't it hurt him?

July 4th, 2020, and a process technician at a dairy plant in northeast Ohio is heading home after a shift that runs from four in the afternoon until four in the morning. It's a thirty-five-mile drive, and the road runs through a long stretch of woods where fog sits most nights, so the driver keeps the brights on and a podcast playing and watches the shoulders for eyeshine, because a deer or a raccoon could step out any second.

About ten minutes after leaving work, a pair of eyes lights up at the side of the road, and a coyote trots out of the trees. That's a surprise all by itself. The driver has seen coyotes before, back home near the old high school, but never out here.
So the car slows down and the coyote starts across, and then, halfway over, it turns toward the headlights and sits down in the road, about ten feet from the bumper.

There's no other car in sight. The driver could just go around it, but it's too strange to drive away from, and surely it's going to get up and wander off any second. It doesn't. It just sits there. So the driver honks.
Two or three seconds go by.
And then the coyote smiles.

The brights are on and it's ten feet away, so there's no mistaking what the driver sees, and the teeth in that smile are human-shaped. Every hair on the driver's body stands straight up. The smile lasts about a second, and then the coyote gets up and runs off into the woods.

For about five seconds the driver just sits there frozen, and then floors it. The plan had been to grab a sausage McMuffin on the way home, and that plan is gone, and so is the driver's appetite, and hours later it still hadn't come back.
The whole rest of the drive goes to second-guessing it, and every time it comes back to the same thing. High beams, ten feet away, clear as day.

The driver has been into the paranormal for years, and is Native American, and the first word that came to mind was skinwalker. Maybe it was that, or maybe some kind of mutated coyote. Either way, the driver was sure of one thing, and that was finding a new way home from work.

Pillar Valley, up in the bush of north-eastern New South Wales, in the late 1990s. A family of four is living in a big shed on their own block of land while the house goes up, a mum and a dad and two little girls, six and ten, and the nearest neighbour is about two kilometres away.

One night, just as they're heading to bed, their Jack Russell starts barking like mad at one end of the shed. The dad opens the roller door into the carport, then one of the two heavy wooden doors to the outside, because the other one's swollen so tight against the concrete it barely moves. The dog shoots out into the tree line, still barking, and a few seconds later it yelps. They hear it running off into the bush, and then nothing.

He spends half an hour out there with a torch, calling for the dog. When he comes back in, his wife and the girls are huddled together in the middle of the room, staring at a window. Something was out there, she tells him, sniffing at the glass.
Before he can say a word, something heavy lands on the roof.

It runs the whole length of it and drops down onto the gravel outside. He hurries everyone upstairs to the bedroom and grabs a machete, and then it's back up on the roof, crawling over to the bedroom window, and they can hear it sniffing. So the whole family squeezes into the tiny bathroom next door and waits.

It jumps down and runs right around the building to the carport, and it hits those wooden doors at full speed and throws both of them open, even the one that was jammed solid. Then it starts banging on the metal roller door, four times, five, before it finally gives up, and they listen to heavy footsteps crunching away across the gravel.
In the morning the roller door is bent inward, and both wooden doors were forced open so hard they gouged the concrete.
The dog turned up two days later. The family lived on that land for about another ten years, and as far as their nephew knows, nothing like it ever happened again. It only had to happen once.

A village in Croatia in the 1980s, with not one streetlight in the village or on the road into town. A teenager walks that road all the time, usually alone, ten kilometres dead straight with open fields on both sides, in pitch darkness, and he's never once been scared.

The first time, he's walking home from a party at three in the morning. On that straight road, about fifteen metres off in the field to his left, there's a man in a hat, standing perfectly still, looking at him.
There's no reason for anybody to be standing in a field at that hour. So he runs the rest of the way home, and he played football his whole life, so he can really run.
The second time, it's around four in the morning, same road, alone again. He's tired, and when he hears two of his friends talking somewhere way up ahead, he runs to catch up.
Every time he runs, they run too. When he stops, they stop. By the time he finally catches them at the end of the road he's mad, and he wants to know why they kept running away from him.
They just stare at him.

Didn't he see the man in the hat? Running through the field right beside him? Every time he started running, they say, the man in the field ran too, right alongside him, coming toward them. That's why they ran.

The third time, he's got a car. It's pouring rain after a party, and he's driving four girls home along that same road through the fields, and about ten metres ahead a man in a hat rises up out of the ditch on the right, runs across the road in front of the car, and drops into the ditch on the left.
He keeps driving, and he doesn't dare look back.
He asks the girl beside him if she just saw a man in a hat cross from one ditch to the other. And she says yes, she did.

It's the afternoon of December 20, 2023, about twelve miles north of Lexington, Kentucky, on a property with a big open field, a pond, a creek nearby and woods along the edge. Close to a hundred Canada geese are resting in the field beside the house.
And then, all at once, every single one of them starts honking and lifts off in a panic.

The owner steps out onto his back deck to see what spooked them, and the first thing he sees is a figure in what looks like all-black clothes walking out into the field. He figures it's a neighbour. Then he realizes it's a bird.

Its back is to him, so he never sees the face. It's jet black and built like a huge hunched vulture, with the shoulders of its folded wings sitting up higher than its head, and he figures it stands five feet tall or more.

He's frozen, torn between running for his phone and not daring to look away, and while he stands there it takes a short run, opens its wings and is in the air after two big beats, the wingtips brushing the grass. The sound is a slow whomp, exactly like the neighbour's little helicopter when the rotor winds down after the engine's cut.

The wings are deep and broad and squared off, with fingered feathers at the tips that look as long as his arm, and he's six foot four. It climbs and clears the trees at the edge of the property by only a few feet, and then it's gone.
Afterward he walks out and paces off the spots where he remembers the wingtips touching the grass. They're sixteen or seventeen feet apart.

His wife and the neighbours say it was just one of the black vultures that roost on the property. But he sees those every single day, and this was three or four times their size. He's stood close to an Andean condor at a wildlife rehab centre in Peru, too, and this was a lot bigger than that.

He doesn't think it was anything supernatural. It moved like a real, flesh-and-blood bird. He used to be a plane spotter as a teenager, he knows wingspans by heart, and he said watching it lift off was like watching a Piper Cub take off from his field.

It's half past ten at night in Australia, and a fifteen-year-old girl is sitting out on her boyfriend's backyard trampoline. His yard sits about a metre above a little park behind the house, so from up there they can see over the fence into the park, faint in the glow of the yard lights.

They're talking, and all of a sudden she goes cold and gets the feeling they're being watched. More than that, it feels like something wants them to know it's watching. She jumps at every sound and he laughs at her.
Then he goes still. He gets up on his knees and stares out into the park, and he says, There's a man watching us from that tree.

It's really tall, he tells her, with its head halfway up a big eucalyptus, and only the head and a shoulder showing, and its eyes are glowing. She half thinks he's teasing her, so she sits up and leans over him to look.
It's there.

It's very tall, and it's darker than the shadows of the trees around it, and the yard lights don't seem to touch it at all. Its eyes are shining bright. She can see a shoulder and an arm draped over the trunk, so she knows it's no animal, and it's way too tall to be a man.

She falls back on the trampoline. He tells her quietly to start heading for the house, because it's coming toward them, but she can't move, and he has to haul her up, swearing, telling her it's almost at the fence. As she scrambles off she catches a glimpse of it, nearly across that short stretch between the trees and the yard.
She bolts for the stairs to the front door, and when she slows down to look back he yells at her not to. It's climbing over the fence.
She made it inside. She guesses it was about three metres tall, with bright, glowing white eyes.
And about a month later, on a late-night video call, her boyfriend told her he could see a figure up in the exposed ceiling beams of her house, watching her.

Just after midnight on January 12, 2008, in Mossley Hill, a leafy part of south Liverpool, an eighteen-year-old is asleep in the spare room at Dad's house when Dad comes in and won't take no for an answer. Get up. Come to the front bedroom. Look at this.

Out the front window, somewhere between a hundred and two hundred glowing balls are moving over the neighbourhood. They look like plasma, maybe fifteen to thirty feet across, mostly orange and red but now and then flickering to green or purple, fifty to a hundred feet above the rooftops. And they're completely silent.
They travel in a line, and the way they move is wrong. One sits dead still, then jumps instantly to something like forty miles an hour to catch up with the one ahead, then stops again.

After about ten minutes Dad goes downstairs for a camera and tells our witness to stay put, because he's worried about what these things might be. Our witness watches alone a few more minutes and then, somehow, ends up back in bed asleep, with no memory of walking back to the spare room.

In the morning Dad fills in the rest. Out in the back garden the orbs were low and bright enough to light the yard, and it was dead quiet, no wind, no insects, no traffic, on a weekend night with the pubs letting out nearby. "Everything felt incredibly silent and still. It felt like being in a separate bubble of reality."
The camera, one they'd used thousands of times without a hiccup, fought him. The first few shots came out pure black. Video wouldn't start, and when it finally did, the file wouldn't play back.

When he finally got a few stills, the orbs looked blue-green instead of orange. And some of them, ones that had been hidden behind the house from where he stood, showed up anyway, fuzzy and faint, as if their light had come right through the building.

Nobody else reported a thing. For about six months afterward the family kept seeing small, high silver-white spheres over the same spot in daylight, appearing out of nothing, multiplying, sliding into one another and shrinking away. A neighbour saw one hang there for eight hours.
Then the family bought a big telescope for the garden, and the visits stopped.
Montana, a fall evening around 1956, a ranch of more than a thousand acres, and the rancher's head count comes up three short. On a spread that size, strays wander back.
But the next morning the teenager who helps him comes into the barn looking green and can barely talk, so the rancher rides out with him to a big shade tree way out on the property.

Under it lie the three missing animals, two cows and a calf. There's no blood anywhere, not one drop, and no bite marks or bullet holes. As he put it, 'Their bellies had been slit open with more precision than a first-class butcher.' He raised beef, so he knew exactly where every organ belonged.

One cow's whole reproductive tract is gone, the edges of the wound slightly charred, and other organs have been neatly put back in the wrong places. The second cow is missing a stomach, her uterus and her tongue, and the vet later finds her brain has been taken out, though there isn't a mark on her head. The calf's eyes are gone, the sockets charred, along with its testicles and a kidney. His horse won't go near the place.

The police take hours to show up and suggest teenagers, then a mother lion teaching her cubs. But there are no tracks except the cattle's own, and the vet can't find any blood left in the bodies or make that charred look happen on a cow that died naturally.

Five or six months later it happens again, more than a dozen head laid out in fresh snow, some with their hind legs cut cleanly off and missing. After that it goes on for years, sometimes a few times a week and sometimes not for months, once twenty-three animals at a time. Hired men patrol at night and see nothing.

In the early sixties it comes closer to the house. He loses hunting dogs, and in 1964 he finds a horse dead and cut up the same way inside its own stall. All told he loses close to two hundred cattle, a few dogs and a couple of horses.
He was a sensible, logical man, and he never did make peace with it. He sold the ranch in the late sixties.

Then, years later, he was watching TV when a show came on about cattle mutilations, and there were ranchers describing exactly what he'd seen. One of them said that on the nights his cattle died, there were strange lights in the sky.

It's a cold January night on his uncle's thousand-acre dairy farm just south of Jacksonville, Florida, moonless and cloudy, about as dark as Florida gets, and two men are out in the cornfields hunting feral hogs. One works the big spotlight and the other shoots. His partner tonight is a friend of his dad's, a Navy chief warrant officer with thirty years in, combat experience and a lifetime of hunting behind him. Not a guy who scares easily.

They hear grunting, hit the light, and there are five good-sized hogs. He drops the lead pig with a clean shot behind the ear and fires a few more rounds as the rest run for the tree line. Ears ringing, they bump fists and start walking toward the downed pig.
On their first step, something screams behind them.

It's long and ragged and furious, loud and close. Think of the morning after you've yelled yourself hoarse at a football game, and then imagine screaming with everything you've got for five seconds. Raw, rasping and almost human, but wrong.
They look at each other, both confused and scared. The officer sweeps the spotlight slowly across the open field and the trees beyond, and there's nothing.
Then it screams again, closer, louder and longer.

The officer asks for his pistol right away and says they need to leave. What about the pig? "Forget the pig." They're a mile from the truck in pitch dark, and a brisk walk turns into a shuffle, then a jog, then a flat-out sprint. He doesn't remember if it screamed again. All he remembers is trying not to fall behind.

Back at the house the other hunters are around a bonfire, and the officer plays it cool, just mentions they heard a funny noise out there. The uncle says raccoons can make some weird sounds. But when they tell him it sounded like a person screaming, he just nods.
He's heard it himself, a few times. Nobody knows what it is. The family just calls it the chupacabra.
It's a regular Midwest winter day around 1980, snow coming down light, and a man is riding the commuter train up from Chicago toward Kenosha, Wisconsin, in a car that's nearly empty.
Now, this man was born in the forties, a dry, devout Christian with zero patience for superstition. Keep that in mind.
As the train slows near Winthrop Harbor, right at the Illinois-Wisconsin line, he looks out the window at a little frozen pond barely ten feet from the tracks.

There are about a dozen small men out on the ice, a foot tall or less. They're dressed in green, some in top hats and some in pointed hats of red and gold, and in his words, 'They were ice skating, doing acrobatics,' gliding around and around that little pond.
He's so stunned he says something to the only other passenger nearby, a woman sitting across the aisle. And she's seen them too.

The two of them sit there and watch together, fascinated and, he admitted, scared, while nobody else in the car seems to notice a thing. Then the train starts moving again and the pond slides out of sight.
His family didn't hear about it until a dinner in 2006, when right in the middle of a conversation about a football game he told the whole thing in a tone you could only call a confession.

The kids tried every explanation they could think of. Maybe it was a trick of scale, and the figures were further off and normal-sized? He wouldn't budge. The pond was tiny, it was right beside the train, and they were small.
And this was the last man in the world anyone would've expected to tell a story like that.

It's 2004, the last night of a camping trip in Joshua Tree National Park, and a few friends are sitting around the fire looking up at the stars. And then a couple of glowing blue objects streak across the sky at crazy speed. He tries to get a picture with his flip phone, but they're way too fast.
Driving home the next day, they can't stop talking about it. Then he notices a black car following them at a distance.
He changes lanes to test it, and it changes lanes with him. Every single time. And the next time he checks the mirror, it's just gone.
The day after that, he comes home from running errands, and there's a black Cadillac parked in his driveway. He tries to tell himself it isn't the same car. His gut says otherwise.

Two men get out and walk up to him. Matching black suits, light grey shirts, black ties, black fedoras. They say they have a few questions about what he saw the night before last, and when he asks who they are and asks for ID, they say they work for a division of the US Air Force.

It's the way they look and sound that he remembers most. Their faces are smooth and blank, almost plastic, a pale olive colour. Their voices are raspy and flat, and they talk in this weirdly precise way that sounds almost synthetic. And their eyes are cold and intense.

They want to know what he saw and what he thinks it was. Did he take photos? Did anyone else have a camera? Has he told anyone who wasn't there? Did he find any unusual debris at the site? And finally, is he holding anything back?
He is. He doesn't answer most of it honestly, and he gives away nothing about who he was with.
They wrap it up by strongly advising him not to talk about it with anyone, and to forget it ever happened. And they make it clear they'll be keeping an eye on him.
For a long time after that he feels watched, and he keeps looking over his shoulder. He's seen a couple more lights in the night sky over the years.
No more men in black, though.
It's around midnight in Chihuahua, Mexico, 2020, and two best friends are cutting across a golf course in the dark, following the cart path.
Up ahead, something comes out of a bush and starts across in front of them.
The first thought is a skunk. There's something pointed and striped sticking up off it like a raised tail, and a skunk is the only thing that makes any sense. "Is that a skunk?"
But the closer they get, the less it looks like one. It's walking on two legs. And it's only about thirty centimetres tall.
Then it notices them.

It turns around with the look of somebody caught in the act, and they hear it gasp. For about three seconds the two friends and this little figure just stand there frozen, staring at each other, and the only thing that moves is its eyes. And they're human eyes, or they look like it.

It has the body of a baby and a tiny adult face. It's wearing nothing but white underpants, like a diaper made out of rags, no shirt, no shoes. Its black hair is piled up in a cone with a thick white stripe down the middle, and that's the skunk tail. Its expressions look almost like a cartoon's.
One of the friends breaks the silence by screaming. "What is that? Is that a child? Is that a baby?"
Because that's what it looks like, something the size of a two-month-old walking across a golf course at midnight.
At the screaming it takes off across the fairway, those little legs moving incredibly fast, and it's gone. Nobody even thinks about following it.
They walk home without saying a word about it, and don't bring it up until the next day. They'd both always been skeptical of duendes, the little people a lot of kids in Mexico grow up hearing about.
That night changed their minds about a lot of things.

Two grown siblings are swapping childhood memories when the oldest brings up something never said out loud before, the creatures that used to show up behind their old house. The youngest, a sister, stops right there. She saw them too, and their stories line up so closely that they both get spooked and change the subject.

The house was in St. Helens, Oregon, with a big stretch of woods out back where the kids played all the time. Every so often the oldest would catch movement at the edge of vision, turn, and there'd be one of two animals nobody could ever name. Never both at once.

The first was tall, dark and very lanky, on all fours and sickly looking, with leathery skin and only a little hair. Something stuck up from its head, big ears or maybe antlers. Look straight at it and it froze. Then it bolted into the trees, and as it ran its outline seemed to blur and shift, like it couldn't hold its shape while it moved, and you could hear the branches snapping.

The second one was scarier. Same long legs, same ears or antlers, but a heavier body and more hair. It always stood somewhere dark, and nobody ever saw it move. If you blinked or looked away, it was gone.
This was the one with a face you could see, huge, milky white eyes with no pupils, watching from between the trees. Both of them were about the size of a big horse.

At first it was terrifying. Before the small one there'd be a feeling of being watched, and before the big one, real dread. But over the years the fear wore off. Our witness started whispering hello to them, and they seemed to stay a few seconds longer after that, and as long as nobody tried to get closer, it felt safer knowing they were out there.

The last clear sighting came on a rainy night after a run of nightmares. Lying awake listening to the rain, our witness let the dark settle, and there was the big one, in the trees outside the bedroom window, its pale eyes standing out against the black.
It was a jolt at first. Then a wave of calm came over, sleep came easy, and the nightmares stopped.
Maybe they were just a couple of strange, sickly animals. That never felt right, though. Both siblings remember them as something that watched over the kids back there.

Late summer in Stoenești, a village in Romania, about eleven at night. It's been raining, and the whole sky is one solid sheet of dark cloud. An eighteen-year-old is sitting on the porch at his girlfriend's family home, facing the house, and she's facing him, with her back to it.
In the middle of the conversation her eyes go wide, and she starts pointing at the sky behind him.
He turns around, and he freezes.

Hanging up there is something shaped exactly like the classic flying saucer, two plates stacked rim to rim. At a glance it could almost pass for a cloud, but it has nothing to do with the clouds behind it. The shape's too perfect. And it just sits there.

It doesn't go anywhere. He thinks it stays put for well over half an hour. His girlfriend runs inside and wakes her dad, and he comes out on the porch and looks up and says right away that it looks like a flying saucer. There's even time for the young man to phone his own father and describe what he's looking at.
Then a second one shows up. This one's directly over their heads.
Neither one makes a sound. They just hover there, the two of them, and after a while they both simply vanish.

He lives about ten minutes away on foot, and he's scared the whole walk home, his head full of every abduction story he's ever heard. On the way he runs into two friends coming back from the bar and blurts out what just happened, and they laugh and tell him to quit lying.

That hits him hard. If friends who know he's no liar won't believe him, who will? His sister is still the only one who believed him from the start, and his girlfriend's father, the other grown-up on that porch, passed away a few years later.
For years he tried not to think about it. Now he's thirty-eight, and he's made a simple animation of the two discs, hoping that somebody, somewhere, saw the same thing.

Rural West Virginia, summer, twenty minutes from the nearest town and miles from any neighbours. Every morning Mom walks the two family dogs down the road, and one morning, about a mile and a half from home, one of the dogs bolts into brush so thick you can't see a thing in it.

From the road she can hear a vicious fight in there, spitting and yowling like a cat, and under it, the mewing of kittens. The other dog stays right by her side. When the first one finally comes back out, he's got a deep gash across his nose.

Everybody at home figures it's a bobcat protecting a litter. So the next day our witness drives out to that same spot with a girlfriend, and coming around the bend, there's a big cat walking along the side of the road.
It's built like a bobcat, with long back legs and big tufts on the cheeks. But just about everything else about it is wrong.

For one, it's big, closer to the size of a lynx. The whole coat is a deep chocolate brown, like a chocolate Lab, with darker bobcat spots still showing through. The ears have long tufts at the tips the way a lynx's do, and there are no lynx anywhere near West Virginia. And the tail isn't a bobcat's little stub. It hangs nearly to the ground.
Then there are the eyes. They're a bright, piercing blue, nothing like a bobcat's dull yellow-green.

The two of them roll along beside it for about ten seconds, only a couple of yards away, and it doesn't hurry and doesn't seem bothered at all. It just glances up at the car, then turns and slips into the brush. Nobody had time to grab a phone.

In all the years since, our witness has never found anything that matches. The best guess is some kind of bobcat and house cat cross, but there isn't much evidence that happens in the wild, and it wouldn't explain the size.
And if that was the mother in the brush the day before, fighting for her kittens, then there could be more of them out there.

Every summer the family went back to Guyana, and Grandpa would come down the river by speedboat to spend a week with them, full of stories about mermaids, shape-shifting river dolphins, witches and dragons. He's Arawak, an army veteran and a conservation ranger and guide who knows the forests of the interior about as well as anyone alive. And the story he told most was the Mapinguari. He swore he'd seen them several times, and when family friends pictured something like Bigfoot, he'd argue. It looked like a tall bear, he said.

In May 2016 his fifteen-year-old grandkid, raised in New York City, goes with him to the village, already wiped out from food poisoning and the long boat ride, and tags along on one of his guided walks with a group of city visitors. Black caimans on the riverbank, tropical birds, a pile of jaguar droppings.

Near the end they come across something odd, a huge mound of dirt and red clay with an opening like a cave. When the visitors ask about it, Grandpa turns it into a joke about the forest having a mind of its own. Then he quietly tells his grandkid they'll be coming back tonight.

After dark the two of them set off with torches and packs. Grandpa's clearly excited. The teenager is exhausted and scared of the jungle at night, and only feels safe because Grandpa walks these forests every day.
The first thing they notice at the mound is the smell, musty and sour, like mildewed wet laundry times ten.
Then off to the left comes a scraping against a tree, and they swing their torches toward it.
About twenty yards away, gripping a tree trunk roughly ten feet off the ground, are what look like enormous bear paws with massive claws.
And then a head leans out from behind the trunk into the light. It looks like a cross between a grizzly and a beaver, with a huge, shaggy, blocky head and big front teeth.
The teenager freezes, then turns to run, and there's Grandpa, laughing, with a hand on the kid's shoulder.
"I tell you de ting look like a bear," he says.

He teases the whole twenty-five minutes back to the outpost, until the teenager calms down, and then he explains. This one's been making a home near the village, and he's been keeping an eye on it for a couple of weeks.

It's 3:30 in the morning in 2007, somewhere in the Midwest, and a veteran is out for a run. He's always put aliens in the same box as Bigfoot, fun to think about, but if they were real there'd be hard evidence by now.
He stops to catch his breath and looks up at a big full moon, about halfway up the sky.
And as he watches, the lower right edge of the moon starts to disappear.

It takes him a second to understand that something is moving in front of it. It's a triangle, a perfect one, with straight sides and sharp points, solid black, with no lights and no sound at all. It slides slowly across the face of the moon until it covers almost all of it, and there's nothing left but three thin slivers of moonlight along its sides.
And then, instead of passing on, it stops.

For about two and a half minutes it turns slowly on its centre point right there in front of the moon, rotating and shifting around like it's dancing, as he put it. Then it rotates back to the left, the way it came, and slides off the edge of the moon.
And the second it leaves the moon, he can't see it at all.

He never saw it coming and he can't see it go, because against the dark sky, with no lights on it, it's basically invisible. The only reason he saw it at all is that it happened to cross the brightest thing in the sky.

It was those sharp corners that got to him most. He'd always figured an aircraft would need rounded edges, and this looked like it was designed that way on purpose. Going by how crisp the edges were, he thinks it was maybe a hundred feet across, and flying low.
Years later he read other people's accounts of silent black triangles, and a lot of them described that same slow, deliberate movement. He doesn't put these in the same box as Bigfoot anymore.

About thirty-five years ago, in a Chicago suburb, a mother is living alone with her four kids, five to nine years old, in a house on a little hill a few hundred yards back from the main road, with about a mile of woods behind it.

It's a late-summer evening and she's getting the kids ready for bed when lights come on outside, like headlights pulling up. That happens sometimes. Then she realizes the lights are shining in through every window at once, from every side of the house.

Total terror hits her, a gut certainty that she and her kids are in danger. She herds all four of them into the big closet in her bedroom, hisses at them to be quiet, and holds the door shut. Her son, the five-year-old, remembers his sister asking about a weird smell. It was their mom's fear-sweat.
Then she hears the front door open, and the back door right after it, and both of them were locked for the night.
Footsteps come through the house. And they come straight to her bedroom, straight to that closet, like whoever it is knows exactly where they're hiding.

And in that instant, she and her son both say, the fear just vanishes, like flipping a switch. She lets go of the handle and the door swings open onto a blinding light. They can't see who's standing in it. But they hear a calm voice say it's the woman in the rocking chair, the gentle presence the whole family believed lived in that house.
That's where her son's memory stops.

She remembers being led out by the hand, with her youngest on her hip and the other kids beside and behind her, walking along willingly toward the lights with two small figures. The hand holding hers was tiny. "Their skin felt like the top of a mushroom."
After that, nothing. They all wake up in their beds the next morning, and her whole body aches.

She was a nurse for more than thirty years and sharp as a tack, and she hesitated for days before she'd tell it. And years later, when her grandkid asked the uncle, the five-year-old from that closet, he told almost exactly the same story. The other three kids only remember bits, the lights, the whispering, the smell, and when it comes up they say they don't remember, and change the subject.

1989, the Royal Palm mudflats out in Palm Beach County, Florida, and ten of them have been mudding all day. Everybody else has gone home when our witness's partner decides to drive through one last small mud hole, just for fun. It isn't small. The truck sinks, and it stays sunk.

Our witness is pregnant, so our witness steers while the other nine push, and they push for more than five hours and that truck doesn't move an inch. There's nobody else left out on the flats. So they give up, three of them squeeze into the cab, the rest settle down in the bed, and they wait for morning.
It's about five in the morning and they're still talking when our witness hears it first, a low, rumbling growl, and tells everybody to hush.
Then they all hear it, and it's getting louder, and angrier.

The partner grabs the big KC spotlight from behind the seat, plugs it in and lights up the night, and behind a big bush something ducks down and moves. And that makes it mad. It stands straight up, lets out a roar our witness can still hear more than thirty years later, jumps that bush and charges right at them. You could feel the earth literally shake with every running step it took.

It's eight or nine feet tall and broad, like a really huge man covered in long, clumped hair, and that spotlight shows every bit of it. And the smell, rotten and sour, and when you're pregnant it's so much worse.

What happens next, our witness puts down to adrenaline. The two guys in the cab jump out and shove against the door frames with the engine running, the seven in the back pile out screaming and push, and with a sucking pop they all still remember, that truck comes free. Everybody throws themselves back in and they tear out of there through those tight wooded turns like the devil himself is behind them.
At a gas station on the main road, all ten of them sit in a row with their backs against the wall, and nobody says a word. They call their parents and get dropped off one by one, still silent.

Our witness and an older sibling who was there that night didn't talk about it for about twenty-five years. When they finally did, and slowly brought the others in, every single one of them remembered it exactly the same way.

West Georgia, early 2020, a rented house at the end of an isolated cul-de-sac, with thick woods starting about ten metres from the back door. The local wildlife office says nothing bigger than coyotes and deer lives out there, and both are shy.

But the two dogs have stopped wanting to go out back at night. They stick close to the house, stiff and alert, and then all of a sudden they lunge at the treeline barking, in a way they never do at rabbits. Some nights they bark at the woods from inside, through the windows.

And the owner can hear it, something walking just inside the trees that doesn't sound like it's on four legs. It's heavy, it snaps branches, and it isn't scared off by the dogs or by yelling. 'If it's there at 9 pm, it'll be there at midnight, and it'll be there at 2am.' In daylight there's no fur, no scat, no scratches and no footprints.
So the owner starts taking a flashlight on every trip outside, and for about a month, nothing new happens.
Then one night the owner is standing at the edge of the patio, with the older dog pulling to go back in, when the younger dog lunges forward, frantic.
The owner looks up, and there it is, standing by one of two big trees at the edge of the woods, half hidden behind the trunk.

Going by branches the owner knows well from yard work, it's about six feet tall. It's covered in light-coloured fur or hair and it's standing upright, but the legs are shaped more like an animal's, and the arms are long for its body. The face is hard to make out, not flat, but not really a snout either.

It lasts a few seconds at most before both dogs get hauled inside, and after that they only go out front. Before long the sounds start coming from the woods across the road too, and on a one in the morning walk to a gas station with a friend, something seems to keep pace with the two of them in the trees, and they get a ride home.

Then the owner hears about a neighbour's husky mix that was let out one night and found the next morning with a broken neck and no other injuries. Maybe that's just a story going around. The dogs stayed on leashes from then on.

It's 1:52 in the morning when the phone rings at home. He's already texted that he's on his way back from work, so a call means something's wrong. At first there's nothing on the line. Then a shaky voice asks if he can be heard. He says he doesn't know what just happened, that he saw something, and he's about to lose signal. Will his spouse please be waiting for him?
So his spouse stands at the front door, watching for headlights coming down their long driveway, and when he walks in he looks stunned.

On his way home he takes an old one-lane road that crosses some abandoned railway tracks. Nobody lives out there, and tonight it's raining. And standing by those tracks are three very tall figures, and one of them is a woman.
They were white, he says, but not white like skin. Snow white. The woman was holding something his brain could only compare to a trash bag with a light inside it, and he knew that wasn't what it was.
They noticed him at the same moment he noticed them. A wave of unease came over him, and all he could think was that he had to get out of there. Whatever they were, he says, they weren't human.

The next morning the two of them drive back out. Right beside the road, by the tracks, there's a black scorch mark on the ground, like something burned there, even though it was raining last night, and it sure doesn't look like anybody had a campfire.

While they're walking back to the car, an old man in a beat-up Ford pulls up and asks what they're up to. Just looking at something, they say. He gets out and chats a bit, and then out of nowhere he asks if they believe in aliens. They look at each other and say yes.
He's lived out that way his whole life, he tells them, and he and his late wife saw plenty of strange things out there. That scorch mark, he says, is from them.
He takes them back to his farmhouse, the one his grandparents built in the 1800s, and from a little shed he brings out five old Polaroids his father took. Every single one is a flying saucer.
He says there are more in the house somewhere.

Thurso is the most northerly town on the British mainland, and in the middle of summer the evenings stay light until around midnight. On the fifteenth of June, 2026, somewhere between ten and eleven at night, a local walks along the town beach and out to the end of the pier to take pictures of the sky, which is a strange colour tonight and shining back off the sea.
The walker is standing out there taking photos when something pushes up out of the water, ten or fifteen metres away.

The first thought is a seal. Grey seals are everywhere in that bay and up the town river, and this walker sees them all the time. But this body is long, much longer than any seal, which runs about five to eight feet.
And the head looks like a seal's at first, but the snout is wrong. It's longer and heavier, and the only thing that comes to mind, of all things, is a hippo.
It stays up for about five seconds. By the time the camera swings around to it, it's almost all the way under, so the one picture shows hardly anything at all.

There were no fins, so it wasn't one of the orcas or dolphins that come through those waters, and it was clearly an animal, no floating log. The walker stood there at the end of the pier and waited for it to come up again.
It never did.

The best ordinary answer anybody can come up with is a young walrus, because every ten years or so one wanders down out of the Arctic into northern Scottish waters, and a walrus would explain that heavy, hippo-like head. But a walrus off Thurso would normally make the local news, and there was never a word about one.
The walker isn't calling it a sea serpent. Just that it wasn't a seal, and that it's the closest thing to a cryptid this walker has ever seen.

It's 2014, nineteen miles out an old logging road in the hills near Hoopa, in Humboldt County, maybe a dozen miles as the crow flies from Bluff Creek, where the Patterson-Gimlin film was shot. A guy, his girlfriend and his buddy are out there for the weekend working on a remote property.

Half joking, he tells them that if you knock on a tree, Bigfoot knocks back. Neither of them wants to hear it, and his buddy, who spent the whole summer out there alone, admits he's heard calls at night he can't place. So of course he grabs a branch and raps on a trunk anyway, and about thirty seconds later, knocks come back from way off in the trees. He figures it's a neighbour messing with them, until his buddy points out the nearest place is nine miles away, in the other direction.
His buddy snores, so the couple pitches a tent down by a little creek below the work area, a nice spot full of frogs and crickets, and they drop right off.
Somewhere around four in the morning he wakes up and everything is silent. No frogs, no crickets, nothing at all.
Then something moves in the brush along the creek, and small rocks start coming up out of the creek bed and pattering against the tent.
He freezes. His girlfriend sleeps right through it, and he doesn't wake her, because he's sure she'll panic.
It comes in rounds, and it goes on for what feels like a couple of hours. The rocks stop, he starts hoping it's gone, and then he hears it pacing along the brush line before the next volley comes in.

Finally he can see the sky going light through the open top of the tent, and the throwing stops. There's a long quiet. And then from down by the creek comes a huge exhale, like an enormous sigh, and something goes crashing off into the woods, and slowly the frogs and crickets start up again.

At first light he stomps up the hill, half sure his buddy pranked them, and he can hear him snoring right through the cabin door. He pounds on it and tells him everything, and his buddy just says he told them there was something strange about this place. Does he believe him now?
He does. Every visit after that, all three of them slept in the cabin, and nobody ever pitched a tent again.

July 2021, two thirty in the morning, a small town in mid-Michigan with cornfields all around it. It's a nice street, houses close together, lots of light, and our witness, who doesn't believe in anything paranormal, is up late like always.

There's a routine. Every night around this time the old Pomeranian comes to the door and huffs, so our witness lets him out the front, and when he comes back they split some ham straight out of the fridge. He's so well trained he doesn't need a leash, and he always comes right back.
Except this night he doesn't hop off the porch. He just stands there, staring across the street, for a lot longer than usual.

When he finally goes, our witness follows his gaze and sees what looks at first like a big dog, maybe a wolf, slinking across the neighbour's lawn about fifty feet away. But it's wrong. It's too long, it moves strangely, and it's blurry somehow, like your eyes can't quite focus on it. And all our witness can think is that if that thing notices an elderly Pomeranian, he won't stand a chance.

So the outer glass door eases open, just enough noise for the dog to hear, and he turns and runs back. And at that exact moment the thing across the road starts turning its head toward the house, slowly and smoothly, almost mechanical, like an animatronic. A feeling comes down hard and all at once that this is something you are not supposed to be seeing.
Our witness looks down for one second to get the dog in and pull the door shut.

When our witness looks back up, the animal is thirty feet to the left, in the neighbour's driveway, standing on its hind legs. It's seven or eight feet tall, it's looking straight at the house, and it hasn't made a sound.
Our witness looks away again, just long enough to lock the door. When our witness looks back, the driveway is empty.

The whole thing took twenty or thirty seconds. Shaking, our witness still gave the dog his ham, and then our witness ran down to the basement to tell a nineteen-year-old brother, just so somebody would know, so there'd be no talking it away in the morning. It was a few restless nights later, searching online, that the word turned up that matched it exactly. Dogman.

January 2024, on a homestead deep in the Appalachian woods of southern West Virginia. The homesteader comes home one day with a strong feeling of being watched, figures it's coyotes after the chickens, and goes out with a gun and the livestock guardian dog, a hundred and fifty pounds of dog, to sit and wait.
The dog's clearly onto something. He lifts his nose, catches the scent and charges toward it, but every time he gets close, whatever it is just seems to vanish. Nothing ever turns up.

The next night the feeling is back. The homesteader takes a light out and shines it along the edge of the woods, and eyes look back. The dog is going nuts, barking and hunting for it, and the thing with the eyes just sits there, perfectly still.
The homesteader walks right up to it. It's a bobcat, ten feet away, staring straight into the light. Then it looks away and calmly walks around a tree like nobody's there at all.

You hardly ever see a bobcat out there, never mind one that lets you walk up and shine a light in its face. The homesteader draws a pistol and pulls the trigger. Nothing. Racks it, tries again, still nothing. "It felt like something was holding my trigger back."

So it's back inside for the shotgun, and then off after the bobcat, about a quarter mile into the woods. It never runs. It just walks, slowly, like it's leading the way somewhere. And the moment the homesteader crosses the tree line, fog rolls in thick, like somebody's aiming a fog machine, until it's impossible to see five feet ahead.

On the way back, through the trees, the homesteader can just make out the fiancée standing on the porch. She's looking back and forth, from the flashlight in the woods to a spot way off behind the house, and she's terrified.

She'd heard the homesteader screaming bloody murder, calling her name and begging for help, from more than a quarter mile off in the other direction. She came out to help, and saw the flashlight nowhere near the screaming.
The homesteader never heard any screaming, and never screamed. The whole time out there, there was only that feeling of being followed and watched by something that could never quite be found.
And it was still early in the night when the homesteader sat down to write it all out. "The night's young," the homesteader wrote, "and I expect it to get weirder."

This bushwalker has spent years camping and fishing in the Australian bush, plenty of nights alone deep in the Blue Mountains, and there've been strange noises, the feeling of being watched, odd stick structures way off any trail. But never a Yowie, and honestly, never enough to be convinced.

So this day it's a long walk with the bushwalker's wife, a long way in, the nearest town about twenty kilometres off. And the whole way in, they keep hearing distant chatter out in the bush, like kids talking and laughing, too faint to make out a word.
About two hours in they turn back toward the car. And the second they do, a single loud knock rings out from the bush, wood on a tree, and they both stop dead.
The wife doesn't believe in Yowies, but she knows the stories, and she jokes that it sounds like a signal, like somebody telling the others they're heading back.
So, half joking, the bushwalker says let's turn around again and keep going, like we never changed our minds.

Five steps. That's all they get before there's another knock, sharp, and close this time, in bush so thick they can only see about ten metres into it. And they notice the birds and the insects have gone quiet.
Now the wife's spooked, and she says that's enough, we're really going back to the car this time.
They turn around. One step, two steps, three.

And then a crack goes off in the bush, loud as a gunshot, louder than anything either of them has ever heard out there. It's a big tree snapping in half and going over, and there's no wind. They never see the tree, they only hear it, and it rattles them so badly that for a moment they both feel disoriented.
Neither of them wants to go look. They walk all the way out to the car talking about the timing, and nothing else happens.
But the message seemed clear enough to them. Stop playing games. You know we're here, and you should leave now.

A dad and his kid are hiking up the side of Mount Shasta, on what they remember as the Old Ski Bowl trail. It's barren up there, a steep slope of rocks and boulders and dirt with hardly a tree on it. About an hour in they pass a group of big boulders set out in a circle. Strange, but they keep going.
They only meet three other people all day. Or at least, that's what they look like.

The first two are another father and son, coming down a steep stretch that runs along a cliff wall. Everybody stops, says hello, chats about the trail, and goes their separate ways. About two minutes later the kid looks back, and that other pair is way down the trail already, on a stretch that should've taken them twenty minutes at least. Nobody else is up there, and their clothes are easy to spot. It's them.

At the top of the cliff there's another stone arrangement off the side of the trail, much bigger than the first, the rocks set out in rows almost like gravestones. A bit further on they'd need climbing gear, so they turn back.

That's when the kid sees a man standing among the rocks, staring at them. Button-up shirt, cargo shorts, a wide-brimmed straw hat. He's close enough that his face should be easy to make out, but it's like he doesn't have one. There's just skin.
The second the dad looks over, the man ducks down behind a boulder, and then peeks back over the top at them, almost playful, like a kid playing hide and seek.
The next few moments are just gone for the kid.

According to the dad, his kid just started walking toward the man, while he called out asking where on earth they were going. The kid came to standing right at the edge of a cliff, above a drop big enough to kill someone.

The dad grabbed the kid, pulled the kid back onto the trail, said stay put, and went down to those boulders to find the man. Nobody was there. And the only ways off that slope were up the trail or down it, and the man hadn't taken either one.

The grandfather in this story was not a man who scared easily. He was raising his younger brothers on his own by the age of nine, rode the rails west at fourteen, worked in a pulp mill around Vancouver and boxed bare-knuckle for extra money. Eventually he and his wife bought a wooded acreage, where he built houses with his own hands and kept horses, dogs and farm animals.

The trouble starts with a horse. His younger daughter, about eight, is riding through the trees on the property when the horse stops dead and won't move. She smells something like rotting garbage and meat, and the moment she pulls the reins, the horse spins and bolts for the house, nearly throwing her. It's never the same animal again.

Then animals start going missing, and one of the hunting dogs is hurt in a night attack. He sets traps and sleeps in the hayloft for several nights with a shotgun and a rifle, expecting a fox or coyotes or maybe a hungry bear. Nothing comes.
The next day his daughter is playing near the treeline with the injured dog when it sniffs the air, puts itself between her and the woods, and starts growling.

Her father comes out, stops, and calls to his wife for his rifle. He's pointing at one treetop that looks thicker than the rest, and it's moving, just very slightly. Whatever's sitting up there is at least six feet tall.
As he aims, a pair of wings begins to open. He fires.

Chest shot, high-powered rifle, and he hears it crash down through the branches. He runs in with the dogs, but where it fell there's only a pile of broken branches. The dogs circle and can't pick up a scent. No body, no blood, no trail. He searches the woods for days and finds nothing, but the animal killings stop.
Decades later, when he's dying, he keeps talking about the thing he saw. He calls it an alien and says it's coming back for him, and the family has never heard fear in his voice before.
A few nights before he dies, too weak to stand by himself, he somehow gets outside with his rifle. His wife wakes to a gunshot and finds him lowering the gun, staring into the dark.

Somewhere in rural Arizona, in a place so quiet at night you can hear a rabbit moving through a bush a football field away, and so dark there's no light pollution at all. Our witness is a keen stargazer, lying in a hammock in the backyard with headphones in, watching the sky.
A single bright white flash goes off up there, like a camera flash. No tail, no streak. Maybe a meteor coming straight at them, they figure.
Then, about fifteen seconds later, the exact same flash goes off in the exact same spot. In all their years of looking up, they've never seen anything like it.
A moment later, something touches their head.

It feels like a hand, almost like it's inspecting their hair, and then it takes one lock at the back of their head and gives it a gentle tug. It's all over in a split second. They're six foot four, two hundred and ten pounds, and they don't scare easily at all, but they sit bolt upright and pull the headphones out, figuring it's their girlfriend trying to get their attention.
She isn't there.
Instead, in that dead-quiet yard, there's a sound that's hard to describe, something like whispering mixed with clicking.

And then the fear hits. An overwhelming, irrational terror, the kind that pins you right where you are. They'd always imagined that if anything like this ever happened they'd keep their cool and try to communicate, and that goes right out the window. The only thing they can compare it to is how a trapped coyote must feel.
They can't really say they see anything. The closest they can get is something like shadow people, there and not there, at the edges.
Frozen, they finally manage to squeeze out a few words. "Okay... please be cool, guys."
The whispering and the clicking stop. The feeling of being watched does not.
Then a big gust of wind comes out of nowhere, and the feeling goes with it, all at once.

It's the fall of 2014 in southeast Missouri, and a family of five is staying with the grandparents on a big open property with views for miles. Two miles to the north is Buford Mountain, a rugged ridge of red granite in Iron County.

It starts one night around eleven, on the front porch, when a huge, bright white light drifts slowly over the house, low enough you could probably hit it with a slingshot. No sound, no shape you can make out. It carries on for about a mile, fades, and it's gone.

Within a week the lights are a nightly thing, and the whole family gathers on the back porch to watch. One evening there are three red balls moving back and forth over the mountain in perfect formation, so tightly synced they look connected. And half joking, the dad starts waving both arms at them.
All three lights immediately turn, and come straight at the house.
The kids get hustled inside. He and the grandparents stay out, and the lights come within half a mile before they split up and shoot off, one west, one east, and one straight up.

But the one that sticks with him most happens on an evening when he and his eleven-year-old son are finishing a game of catch in the front yard. A red ball of light is hanging silently near the peak. It slides east over the summit, stops dead, comes back, pauses, and parks just west of the peak.
And then it starts to pulse.

With every pulse, a big circle of red light lights up a patch of the mountainside. Two flashes, then four more, six separate spots in quick succession, like it's working through a grid. Then it shoots off and vanishes in a flash.

He's an Air Force veteran with a physics degree, and lighting up the ground that clearly from two miles away takes a lot of power. Power like that comes with noise, engines, rotors, turbines. This was completely silent.

The day after that light gets reported, he's home alone when the house starts shaking. He gets to the glass doors just in time to see two black military helicopters roar over at treetop height, west to east, and then they're gone behind the trees.
One pass. They never came back.
There's a big cattle ranch outside a tiny, middle-of-nowhere town in northern Nevada, run by the same family for generations, and in all that time nobody had ever found anything like this.
On the morning of December 23rd, 2024, a brother-in-law comes across a dead bull in one of the fields. Going by the body, it died just after dark the night before.

Its cheeks have been cut off, along with its tongue and the tip of its right ear, cuts that look like knife work. On its ribs there are dash-shaped marks that look burnt, sitting right over the ranch's brand. There's a large swelling on the neck where it lies, and they look for an injection site but can't find one.
And then there's what isn't there.
There's no blood.

And in a place full of coyotes and ravens and every other scavenger, nothing will touch the carcass. Three days later they go back out to it in the weeds and photograph it again, and it's still lying there, untouched.

Some of it points to plain old foul play. Some strangers stayed at a local motel that night, and the sheriff's office is following up on it, and pieces of the bull have been cut off and frozen for testing. But the family can't make the rest add up. If someone was after meat, why take the cheeks and tongue and leave a whole bull? If it was poisoned, why cut it at all? And why burn new marks over an old brand?
The older generation wants to keep the whole thing quiet. The younger ones want answers. And it's the missing blood and the scavengers keeping their distance that keep the family up at night.
"Where is the blood? Why won't anything eat the carcass?"

October 2005, the Mojave Desert near Joshua Tree, and a big guy with a shotgun and a friend's Jack Russell is walking back to his Jeep along one of those endless dirt roads after a day of quail hunting. He's a medical professional, an outdoorsman and a biology nerd, comfortable in the dark and not the type to panic, and it's full twilight.
At a crossing marked with stop signs, the terrier freezes mid-trot, hackles up and growling, and that easygoing dog never does that. His first thought is javelina, and all he's got is birdshot.

On the far corner of the crossing, about forty feet away, something is walking with a rooster's strut, minus the head-bobbing. It's about three feet tall and, going by its bulk, forty or fifty pounds. He clips the dog's leash to his belt and waits for it to move along.
It hangs around on the corner for a minute.
Then, without a flap or a sound, it jumps about nine feet straight up from a standstill and lands perfectly on top of the stop sign.

He loads two fresh shells, and when he looks up he sees its eyes, and the biologist in him clocks two things at once. They face forward, which means predator. And they're huge for its size, which means it hunts at night. So now there's a silent, nocturnal, forty-pound predator that can jump nine feet, looking down at him from a high perch.
He fires both barrels.

When the echo dies, it's still sitting on top of the sign, making odd little chirruping sounds that sound a lot like sneezing. While he reloads, it hops down and runs off through the brush on the next corner.
Later he drove back and put his lights on that sign, and it was peppered with shot, most of it right where the thing had been sitting. Two loads of birdshot at forty feet, and it sneezed at him.

Manchester, around 1953. A young mother has given birth to her son at home just a few hours ago, and now she's lying in the dark with the baby fussing on her chest, and she can't sleep. The only light comes from the streetlamps, through the net curtains.
Slowly, she gets that prickling feeling of being watched.
Then she hears whistling, right beside the bed.

She looks down, and on the floor to her right there's a tiny man in a suit and a top hat, grinning up at her. He's full of mischief, almost mocking. He points at her and at the baby and makes a big belly-laugh gesture, dances from one foot to the other, and tips his hat.
And then he jumps up onto the bed.
He comes closer, still laughing, still pointing at the two of them, and a deep dread comes over her, like this little man knows something she doesn't and he's gloating about it.
So she shuts her eyes, and tells herself it's exhaustion, and eventually she falls asleep.
Her son died young, in 1980.
For the rest of her life she was convinced the little man had known that was coming, that night in the dark when her baby was only a few hours old.
And that all that dancing and laughing beside her bed was him celebrating.

It's three in the morning in a small California town, and the streets have been empty since ten. A college student who works the night shift at a Jack in the Box has been sent home early, and stops for gas on the way to save time before morning classes.
It's a tiny station. Two pumps, no attendant, barely any light, and nobody around.
Or so it seems. Getting out of the car, the student notices a man standing about twenty feet away, in front of the outdoor ice machine.
He's tall, and very pale, and bald. He's wearing a full suit and a long coat, and he's holding a briefcase.

Nothing about him fits. The night isn't cold enough for that coat, and the outfit's way too formal for a town like that. There's no other car on the lot, and the station isn't anywhere you'd walk to. He doesn't smoke. He doesn't check a phone. He doesn't look around.
The whole time the gas is pumping, he just stands there in front of the ice machine without moving, and he never once looks over.
The student keeps an eye on him all the way back into the car, and pulling out, takes one last look in the rear-view mirror.
And right at that moment, almost like he felt it, the man starts walking off into the dark, in the same direction the car is going.
There's nothing out there for him to walk to.

The student takes a different road home, just in case, and never sees him again. Friends have always said it was probably just some guy, and maybe it was. But years later, reading other people's stories about pale, oddly formal men in suits turning up in empty places, it started to make a different kind of sense.

In a farming province of the northern Philippines there's a traditional house up on stilts, built in the 1950s, with dark hardwood floors and a springy bamboo kitchen floor you can see the ground through. Rice-farmer grandparents live there with four grown children, the yard is closed in by eight-foot walls, and everybody's washing goes on the same lines.
The youngest daughter, Ella, is about twenty-one when she notices her underwear keeps disappearing from the line. Only hers. Never anyone else's.
She blames a prankster sibling, then questions everybody, the maids too. Nobody owns up. They watch the washing for birds or animals, and still the gaps show up, week after week.
Fed up, the grandfather calls in a local manghuhula, a seer. She walks the compound and announces that the family aren't the only ones living there.
