A small family of dwende, the little people of Filipino folklore, lives under the coconut trees, she says, and their territory reaches right under the house. And one of them has taken a fancy to Ella.
She leads the family down under the house.
And there's every missing piece, folded neatly and tucked away into the cracks.

The seer blesses the house with coconut oil and prayers to move the dwende on, and tells the family to paint red crosses on the stilts and the walls underneath, and to put white crosses in the windows.
Years later, a grandchild found those red crosses as a small child, and that's how the story finally came out. The house still stands, crosses and all.

It's November on the north shore of Lake Superior, and a couple has booked two nights in a primitive cabin past Grand Marais. Wood stove, wood-fired sauna, no running water. And mirrors, small hexagonal ones at chest height, six on each wall, every one facing a mirror on the opposite wall. That's what bothers the hunter who booked it.

This is somebody who spends months outdoors every year and doesn't spook easily. But once the sun goes down there's a feeling of being watched that won't go away, and the girlfriend feels it too. Twice the hunter opens the doors and calls out into the dark. Then both of them hear footsteps on the roof, walking back and forth over the bedroom.

That night they have the same nightmare. The hunter dreams of a town flooding during a search for a grandfather, with a shadowy man standing behind, one hand on the dreamer's shoulder. The hunter wakes to find the girlfriend staring back, starts describing it, and she finishes it, the rising water, the figure behind, and her own screaming that nobody heard.
At about three thirty in the morning the outhouse door slams so hard they both sit bolt upright. The hunter opens the back door, and the motion light is already on, and there's no wind at all.

The next afternoon, in the sauna, the hunter feels someone right behind the door and starts talking to the girlfriend. Nobody's there. Back in the cabin she's doing the dishes and talking too, sure her partner is standing behind her.
When they compare notes later, they've both pictured the same thing out there. A horribly thin human figure with a skull-like face, glowing white-blue eyes, and a crown of antlers.

The car's packed before dark. Waiting for the girlfriend, the hunter feels a strong urge that doesn't feel like the hunter's own, to just drive off and leave her there. Instead the hunter goes back and finds her crying on the back porch, and they have a furious argument neither one can remember the reason for.
On the way out, a big white wolf crosses the road in the headlights, stops to look at them, and walks on. The further they drive, the calmer they feel.
Later the hunter emails the owner, suggesting only that someone check the roof and the outhouse door for noises. The reply is a single question. "What sounds did you hear?"
The couple believe it was a wendigo. And the hunter is sure that if that car had pulled away without her, she'd have become a missing-person case.

It's late at night in Buena Park, out in the Los Angeles and Orange County sprawl, and there's a big family party going. The kids are bouncing in an inflatable jumper out front, the adults are singing in the backyard, and a long driveway runs down the side of the house, so the front gate is in plain view of everybody at the back.
For no particular reason, one of the kids wanders over to stand by the front gate and looks straight up.
Hanging right over the party is a disc, exactly like a flying saucer out of an old movie, spinning, with a ring of lights around its edge.
After a few seconds it shoots away to the north-north-east.
Our witness looks down to the left, and there's a sister, staring up too. 'Did you see that?' She nods.

But the other kids are still playing, and nobody at the back has reacted at all. So the two of them go around asking if anyone else saw it. Their mum puts it down to overactive imaginations, and the pair, who love making up stories, soon turn it into a game about a Disney ride you could sit inside.

Years later, all grown up, our witness asks the sister about that night, and her eyes go wide. She remembers looking up, and the disc, and realizing nobody else had noticed, and the story they made up afterwards. The only thing she doesn't remember is it zooming away.
A crowded yard in one of the busiest parts of Southern California, a whole party going on right underneath it, and apparently only two kids saw it.
And it isn't hazy like a dream. It feels like any other real memory from childhood.

August 2010, a few miles outside Crater Lake National Park, and a couple has pulled off on a forest road near the Rim Drive to camp. No campground, just them and the car. They walk down a slope toward a little ravine where they can hear water running.
On the way back up the gentle incline toward the car, Grandma stops dead and grabs his arm.
About fifty yards up the slope, near the top of the ridge, something is standing perfectly still and looking down at them. It's upright, dark brown or nearly black, and at least eight feet tall.

Grandpa grew up hunting, and every time he tells it he comes back to the same line. 'It wasn't a bear.' The arms are too long and the shoulders too broad, and while it studies them it tilts its head, just a little. 'Too human, but not,' he says.

Grandma panics. She starts crying, turns her face away so she doesn't have to look at it, and begs him to get back to the car. He stands frozen for what feels like a full minute while his brain tries to make sense of something it has no picture for.
Then it turns. It doesn't bolt. It just walks smoothly back over the ridge, no crashing in the brush, no sound at all, and it's gone.

They never reported it. Grandpa started reading instead, and in the fifteen years since he's filled whole binders with maps, sighting reports, weather records and local legends from the southern Cascades. He's a grounded, practical man, and he's convinced there's more going on in those forests than most people realize. A couple of times a year he still drives back and walks that same slope, still looking.
Grandma won't talk about it at all. She won't even look at the binders.

January 2019, a neighbourhood about seven miles out of downtown Scranton. The front of it faces a main highway, but behind the houses it's all state game lands, and the turkeys and deer and what seems like every skunk in the county come wandering through.

One night our witness catches movement on the driveway from a window that looks down over it. Something is walking slowly toward the street on all fours, nose to the ground, swinging its head from side to side. A bear, probably.
So our witness moves to the bedroom window, which looks straight out over the street, and watches it come down to the road.
And then it stands up.

In one easy motion it's up on two legs, walking out into the street with its head up, sniffing the air, and under the yellow streetlight the silhouette is clear. Tall pointed ears and a long snout. Long claws on hands that hang loose at the wrist, arms that would reach below the knee, dog-like legs, and it's walking up on its toes. Going by the streetlight, it's seven to seven and a half feet tall.

It strolls across the road and crouches down in a thick tangle of scrub on the other side, and that's when our witness realizes it's looking straight into the bedroom window. Its eyes look blue, and there's no telling if that's reflected light or their own glow.

Our witness's legs just give out, and that's it, sitting hard on the floor under the window, home alone with five cats and a dog that sleeps through the whole thing, behind a big picture window that wouldn't stop anything.
When our witness finally gets up on both knees and peeks over the sill, the eyes are gone. Maybe it went back toward the game lands. Maybe it just settled down in the scrub.

It never acted aggressive, not even while it was watching. But in the months after, there was tapping at the windows and scratching on the siding, and the seven stray cats that used to come around for food disappeared, one by one.
For anybody out there hoping to see one, our witness has some advice. Pray you never do.

It's about a quarter to three in the morning at a house out in the country, and a five-month-old puppy needs to go out again. So his owner, a young healer raised on the old ways by a Cherokee grandmother, takes him into the back yard under a huge, nearly full moon.
While the puppy sniffs around, the healer slowly realizes there are no night sounds at all. Then the puppy growls, low, and presses against the healer's legs, tail tucked, hackles up.
At the edge of the yard there's what looks like a coyote. But this one looks wrong and feels wrong, and it's staring straight at the two of them.

In the moonlight it's clear. Its fur is thin and bald in places, and its eyes are yellow like the sun, almost blinding. Its back legs are longer than any canine's should be, and from the hips down it looks built for walking upright.
Without looking away from it, the healer scoops up the sixty-pound dog and silently says a Cherokee prayer the grandmother taught. The thing backs up a little, like it's physically upset.
And then it speaks, in a perfect copy of the grandma's voice. 'Why would you do that, Mikkers?' Only the grandparents ever called the healer that.

The healer runs inside with the dog and locks the door. The brother comes in, annoyed at the noise, and the two of them switch off the lights and creep into the living room. Through the stained glass in the door there's the outline of something tall and human-shaped. Then the knob starts to turn.

The brother grabs it and locks it just in time, and then it talks to him in their grandpa's voice. 'Bubba, why don't you let grandpa in?' Their grandparents are hundreds of miles away, on the reservation in Cherokee, North Carolina. The brother goes white.

The next night, same time, the tapping on the glass comes back. The two of them sit praying, and the more they pray, the harder it pounds, until their dad, a lifelong skeptic, storms over thinking it's the brother's friends and throws the door open.
It doesn't come at him. It drops to all fours and runs off down the road, and their dad stumbles back, pale, locks the door and goes to bed without a word.

The next day, following the grandmother's instructions, they sprinkle juniper ash around the house, and it never comes back. But the dog was never the same, and even now, in his new home, he won't go outside at night.

It's around 1989, in the hinterland behind Queensland's Sunshine Coast, and the family's house backs onto a wooded hill. Everyone's asleep except the sixteen-year-old, who's lying awake listening to the drizzle.
Then come the footsteps.

Heavy, deliberate thuds, walking up the side of the house, like someone following the line of the awning to stay out of the rain, splashing through the puddles as they go. The rhythm's wrong for a kangaroo. The rest of the family sleeps right through it, and the teenager lies frozen as the steps pass right by the open bedroom window.
Within seconds, whatever it is has climbed the eight-foot embankment behind the house toward the treeline, about twenty metres from that window.
And from up there comes a roar.
It's guttural, and it rolls right across the valley, swinging between high and low pitches in a few seconds, and it's so loud the teenager feels it hit like something physical.
On the far side of the valley, about two kilometres away, the neighbours' dogs go wild. Nobody had ever heard those dogs before that night, and nobody ever heard them again.
It's ten or fifteen minutes before the teenager can move, and only because Dad's up and in the kitchen. He heard it too, and he isn't sure what to make of it.
Years later, listening to recordings of supposed yowie and bigfoot calls, our witness recognised the sound straight away, and has no doubt now that a yowie walked past that house in the rain.
There's a small town in western Maryland that, according to somebody who grew up there, is very, very weird.

When our witness was little, there was an imaginary friend named Sarah, a blonde girl of maybe ten or eleven with green eyes and a white and blue Victorian dress. Then the family moved a few streets over, and in the new house a shadowy figure started following the kid around, more and more often. Our witness named him the top-hat man.

He never did anything except follow and watch, but he was terrifying, standing there in the corner of the bedroom. And every time he showed up, Sarah wasn't far behind, and as soon as she came, he left.

The last time was around grade six. Our witness is at the dining room table doing homework, the top-hat man is watching from across the living room, and Sarah is perched on the end of the couch between them, like a guard dog.
And this time he opens his eyes. They're dark red.
He starts toward the table in silent jerks. Sarah stands up and puts out her hand, and when the two of them touch, they're both just gone.

That was the end of it, until years later, when our witness was fifteen and walked into the little sister's room and found her looking terrified. She was eleven. It took a while to get it out of her, but she kept seeing a shadowy man in a top hat. And a little girl she called Sarah.

For months she came to her older sibling in tears, saying he was watching her, in the bedroom, in the kitchen, once even at their grandmother's house. Then the family had the house blessed for other reasons, and she never brought it up again.

But here's the part that gets to them both. Swapping ghost stories at sleepovers and lunch tables all through middle and high school, ten other kids from that same town described the exact same thing. A tall shadow in a top hat, a little blonde girl named Sarah, and the visits stopping around age eleven or twelve.
Snow hardly ever falls on the BC coast, so one winter evening, just after sunset, two siblings and their boyfriends run out into the backyard to play in it.
Then the sister freezes.

Behind a tree, she says, there's something big sitting there, with black wings folded down around its hunched body, watching them. She starts walking toward it, and it turns and covers its face with a wing, then moves behind the tree, and it's gone.
Nobody believes her. A raven, they say, or a heron, or a shadow. But she's badly shaken, so they all go inside.

A few months later the same four are in the main bedroom, with its French doors opening onto a sundeck over the yard. Our witness's boyfriend opens the doors and sees an enormous bird drop off a branch in a tree on the bank behind the yard. 'Holy shit, that eagle is huge,' he says.

Our witness looks up in time to see it fly for a couple of seconds before it vanishes behind more trees. There are eagles all over that coast, but this is far bigger, and completely black, with a wingspan they estimate at nearly fourteen feet.
To our witness it looks like a person with wings, and the boyfriend, who doesn't believe in any of this, says the same thing.
Then the sister reminds everybody about the thing behind the tree in the snow, and this time they all believe her.
And they remember the family's old dog, who died that January, growling and pacing on the deck at night at something out in the yard.
A house out in the countryside, forest all around and no close neighbours, and our witness lives there alone.

In the middle of the night our witness wakes up all at once, not drifting awake but jolted, because something has hold of their right ankle. Hard. It lifts the leg up to about a fifty degree angle and starts dragging them toward the foot of the bed.
They're lying on their stomach and can't twist around to see, and the first thought that comes is a break-in. Our witness is furious. Who the hell is in the bedroom?

Our witness tries to yank the leg back and reaches behind to grab whoever it is, and every time a hand gets close, the grip jerks hard and straightens the leg out again. Five times, six times, and then the hand just lets go.
They roll over expecting to see an intruder standing there. At first the room looks empty.

Then, by the window at the end of the bed, there's a tall black figure shaped like a person, half crouched like it has to duck under the ceiling. It's hunched, with two long arms, and its head is tilted a little to one side like it's curious, like it's studying them.

It's no shadow. It's blacker than the dark in the room, like a hole cut out of the world, soaking up the light instead of reflecting it. And it sparkles. The whole surface of it shimmers with tiny blinking specks, almost like glitter, thousands of little reflective flakes shifting as it moves.
There's nothing pretty or magical about it. It just looks like something that isn't entirely solid.
They stare at each other for several seconds, and then it's gone.
Our witness is still wondering what it wanted.

It's late July 2019, just after eleven at night, on the edge of a town north of Toronto where the houses give way to farmland, and it's garbage night. Our witness grew up in Trenton, an air force town, made a couple of hundred freefall skydives, and is used to judging aircraft at height.
And sitting just above the treeline, there's an orange light.

At first it looks like a streetlight. Then it looks like a Chinese lantern. But it keeps getting bigger as it comes closer, low and slow, under a thousand feet, until it's less than two kilometres away.
And everything goes silent. Even the crickets stop.

It's about the size of a house. The surface looks like lava, rippling like boiling water out from a darker spot in it like a bruise. And fast, sharp-edged pulses of energy, about four a second, are running over the whole thing at once.

It moves north to south past the house, and then it starts to rise. It climbs to somewhere between five and ten thousand feet, and then it disappears, with a low popping sound and three or four echoes.
The whole thing lasts about three minutes, and the phone video only catches a point of light.
Our witness doesn't know what it was, but is sure it wasn't a plane, or a helicopter, or a balloon, or a drone, or a lantern, or ball lightning.
And has been looking up ever since.

Somewhere in the Pacific Northwest there's a stretch of forest that one parent picked off a map, figuring that if Sasquatch was real, it couldn't be that hard to go find one. So every day while the kids are at school, the parent walks it.

Over a hundred-plus hours out there, there are stick structures, bent trees and footprints, from fourteen inches up to twenty-three, and once a single print twenty-six inches long, like a whole family. Hang around one spot too long and small rocks come flying out of the brush.

Only once does the parent actually see one. Looking downhill, something runs upright for three strides, then drops to all fours and dives into a stand of trees with a pale flash from the soles of its feet. The panic is unlike anything before or since.

The parent has read that these animals come closer to people with kids, so the kids start coming along. On the first trip the six-year-old son stands at one of the stick structures for about a minute, and then something hidden in the bushes starts bellowing at them, loud and furious, like two big animals at once.

The next day the parent goes back with the boy and his eight-year-old sister. After a picnic lunch a horrible stench rolls in on the wind, like a dead dog in a sewer. The boy wants to leave, but the parent talks the kids into walking over to a muddy spot nearby.
And there are the freshest prints ever, three tracks crossing over each other, with the mud around the big toe still sharp. Minutes old, the parent figures.

Then it clicks. The smell is coming from the opposite direction to where the prints are headed, which means whatever made them has circled around behind. The boy figures it out almost instantly and runs.

As they hurry after him, the parent tells the daughter to watch the thickets downhill, and she stops. She can see one. It was watching her brother run, she says, and it froze when it noticed her looking.

When she glances back it's standing upright, holding a rock it's just picked up. It seems to realize she can still see it, and its face changes. The brow furrows and it bares its teeth, the tendons in its neck stand out, and its cheeks flush red as its breathing gets heavier.
It raises the rock, but it never throws it. She tells her parent it's really angry and they need to go.
So they go.

It's around midday on Monday, October 18, 2021, and a parent is walking two little boys, seven and two and a half, along a half-mile trail beside a creek in a small state park a mile and a half from home. They hike here every week. The trail ends at a fork in the creek, with a tiny beach about twenty feet long.

Like always, the seven-year-old runs on ahead and gets to the beach a few seconds before the others. The little one starts tossing rocks into the water on the left, the big one does the same off to the right, and their parent bends down to cuff a pant leg.
Then the seven-year-old screams.
It's bloodcurdling, and he's falling over backwards, kicking his legs. The parent follows his eyes across the creek.

On a big flat rock on the far bank, no more than twenty or twenty-five feet away, there's an animal that makes no sense. It looks big enough to clear the creek in one jump. It's got a barrel chest, and the chest and shoulders and arms are muscled like a man's, only much bigger. The eyes bulge, the snout is short and stubby like a hyena's, the ears point forward, and there are tufts of hair on the sides and top of the head.

And it isn't on all fours. It's crouched like a sprinter in the blocks, on heavy thighs and haunches, and its head keeps snapping back and forth between the screaming boy and the parent, alert like a dog waiting for a ball to be thrown. It looks like it's about to lunge, or about to back off.

The parent scoops up the toddler, gets between the thing and the older boy, and gets back onto the trail out of its line of sight, yelling at the seven-year-old to run. He sprints thirty feet, sobbing, then stops and turns around in a daze, like he doesn't understand what's happening, and has to be told again. That happens three times.
The animal never follows.
There's a knife on the parent's hip, and it feels about as useful as a pillow. "It was the only time in my life I knew I could not protect my children."
But the thing that left the deepest scar wasn't even the animal. It was telling a seven-year-old he might have to grab his little brother's hand and run for the car on his own.

Winslow, Arizona, sits about five miles south of the Navajo Nation, and when our witness was growing up there, skinwalkers were something people talked about and took seriously. Plenty of locals had stories, and by the time our witness left town, there were a few more.

At thirteen, it was a man standing in an alley behind the house, one our witness and two friends had to swerve around while running from a patrol car. Three minutes later they ran back the same way. The man was gone, and sitting in the exact same spot was a coyote, calmly watching them. They ran right past it, feet away, and it held its ground, and coyotes never let you get that close. All three of them stayed indoors for a month.
The last one is on the road to Starlight Pines.

Our witness is fifteen or sixteen, riding with an older brother in his Chevy S10 to see his girlfriend, twenty-five miles south of town through nothing but desert and forest. About fifteen miles out they pass a man standing by the side of the road in a flannel shirt and jeans. Odd, out there, but he looks normal enough.
They stay with the girlfriend's family until late, then head home the same way. Hours have gone by, and the man is standing in the exact same spot.
As they pass him, something hits the back of the truck with a loud bang.

The brother starts to slow down, worried about damage, and in the brake lights our witness sees the man. He's running after them down the road, feet from the tailgate, and they're doing fifty-five or sixty.
'Don't stop! Gun it, man! Gun it!'
The brother floors it, all the way to eighty, where the S10's governor won't let it go any faster. And for two miles the man keeps up. Then all at once, he's gone.
They get home and run inside to tell their parents. The next morning, looking the truck over, they find a handprint smeared in the dust, running across the tailgate to the right taillight.
They never drove that road at night again.

It's a spring afternoon on a family farm in Australia, a couple of hundred acres, most of it bush, with a few paddocks for the cows. A thirteen-year-old has spent hours out at a favourite spot in the scrub, building little shelters and fires.

Around four, a call echoes across the property. It's high-pitched, like a hyena laughing, and it goes on for a solid five seconds. It sounds far off, and there's a pocket knife handy, so the teen stays put.
Around six, walking home for dinner, the teen hears something heavy crunching through the brush off to the right. Kangaroos sound like that, so it's worth a look.
And through the trees there's what looks like a tree trunk standing there. Until it moves.

It walks around a patch of bush in odd stops and starts. It smells wild, like an animal, though not as foul as some of the stories say. And it's making noises to itself the whole time, muttering and rambling, and every now and then a high-pitched little huff, like "hm?"
It crosses about thirty metres in front of our witness, and then it seems to look straight over. It freezes.
And it shows its teeth.
This kid is big on animals, and knows exactly what that is in a primate. It's a threat.
Then it's off up a steep bank to the left, snapping branches as it goes, and as soon as the noise fades the teen runs harder than ever before, stopping only to catch a breath and check the treeline.
That's when one more call comes, a high howl with a kind of animal laughter at the end of it.
The parents figured it was a deer or a kangaroo. Their kid couldn't sleep properly for days.

It's an evening at the very end of June 1977, or maybe the start of July, and a man from Golub-Dobrzyń in northern Poland, the grandfather in this story, is walking his guard dog in the forest on the edge of town. The woods there are cut through with old, collapsed trenches from the war.
About ten metres from one of those trenches, the dog stops and stares. And a man climbs out.

He's young, early twenties at most, tall and lean, with a mane of dark wavy hair and a goatee. He's wearing a dark wide-brimmed hat with feathers in it, a green cloak patterned with leaves, dark jackboots and heavy gauntlets. And his eyes are wide, and they aren't light brown. They're the colour of molten gold.

The two of them stare at each other in surprise. The castle in town is about to hold its first knights' tournament re-enactment, so the grandfather asks if the stranger's there for that and got lost. The stranger answers in a language he doesn't know. It isn't German or English. To him it sounds like something Romance.
The stranger points at the growling dog and asks something, and before the grandfather can answer, the dog breaks its leash and charges.
The stranger lifts a hand and points one finger at it, and a burst of purple light flashes underneath him with a bang like a huge firework. The dog turns and runs off yelping.
Then the young man looks at the grandfather with what seems like disappointment, and guilt, flicks his wrist, and vanishes in another purple flash and a sudden gust of wind.
The grandfather runs home, and the dog is already waiting at the gate.

Around two the next morning he wakes with a strong urge to look out the kitchen window. Out in the yard, by the garage, there's a dark outline standing there, with the same golden, glowing eyes. It seems to gesture. It holds his gaze for a few seconds, and then it disappears in a glowing purple circle and a gust that shakes the branches.

He was a rugged, practical man who didn't read fantasy, and he was deadly serious whenever he told it. And he said that for years afterward, the plants on that exact spot by the garage always grew taller than the rest.

Way up in the north of New Hampshire, in Coos County, most of the crowd staying at a friend's family cabin has gone off to shoot at a sandpit up the road. Our witness and a girlfriend aren't into that, so a buddy who's heading out fly fishing on his own invites the couple along.
They saw moose earlier near Pittsburg, so on the way the three of them decide to go moosing. The buddy crawls the car along the back roads while everybody peers into the tree line.
Before that day, Sasquatch had never once crossed our witness's mind.
Then out of nowhere the buddy slams on the brakes, and all three of them yell the same word at the exact same moment. Sasquatch.

A huge, hairy, upright figure is crossing the road ahead of them, about seven feet tall, with long arms and brown hair. It moves so smoothly it almost seems to glide, and it steps into the trees at the side of the road. The whole thing takes maybe two seconds.
They drive up to where it went in. They can see a hundred feet into those woods, and there's nothing, no sign of anything big moving away.

And then there's the part that still bugs our witness. About twenty yards further on, a man and his kid are standing in a front yard. The three of them roll slowly past, stunned, sure he must have just seen the same thing, and the man just stares back at them, and nobody says a word.
They turn the car around twice on that stretch and see nothing more. Back at the cabin, out of that whole big group, exactly one person believes them.

Five years later it still comes up in our witness's head almost every week. This is somebody who thinks most of the footage online is fake, who has run through every skeptic's question there is, could it have been some kind of shared illusion, why has nobody ever caught one. But it always hits the same wall.
Three people saw the same thing at the same moment, and all three shouted the same word.

Late summer 2018, the mountains of north Georgia, all steep ridges and hollows choked with mountain laurel, right up against a big stretch of national forest. It's in the high nineties, and a land surveyor is out there working alone. Twenty years in the woods across five states, completely at home out here, carrying a pistol every single day.

The surveyor has just spent a good long while with a machete, hacking a five-foot-wide sight line up the property boundary to the top of a ridge, three hundred and fifty, four hundred feet. Then it's back down to the bottom to set up the instrument, headphones in, podcast playing.
Looking back up the line, there's somebody near the top, walking slowly across the opening.
It looks hairy, and it seems to be wearing a hat. It stops, reaches up with a big hand and grabs a branch on the tree beside it, and looks down the line.

First thought, a hiker. That happens now and then. But it's way too hot for the shaggy brown jacket it seems to have on, and as it keeps staring downhill, the surveyor can make out pointed ears on top of its head, and a long snout. Then it turns and walks slowly out of sight.
Out come the headphones, and only then does the surveyor notice the woods have gone dead silent. In a Georgia summer the bugs are deafening. Now there's nothing.

The gear's still up top, and after a few minutes the surveyor makes the climb, thinking seriously about just leaving it there. The brush is pushed over the way the figure went. And then there's the tree it walked behind, and that low branch it reached up to grab is about six feet off the ground. The jacket was fur. That's when the fear really lands.

Something is moving a short way off, right where it went. So the surveyor starts the forty-five-minute walk back to the truck, and the whole way, up on the ridge above, something is moving along too, keeping pace. There's no stopping to find out if it's following.
And here's what sticks. Just minutes before, the surveyor had been standing up on that same ridge, back turned, podcast playing, probably within a few yards of it.

November 2020, a trailer in the middle of nowhere in Utah, at least twenty miles from the nearest town, with a reservation about two hundred feet past the property line. Two buddies live out there, and over a few days, things start going wrong.

Their truck starts to stink of sulfur and rotten meat, and then the trailer does too, and they keep that trailer spotless, and there isn't any meat on the property. At night they hear scratching and knocking, which makes no sense that far out.

One night they decide to go find whatever it is. About two miles from the truck they catch the smell of sulfur, and then they both see it, a silhouette six or seven feet tall, running straight at them.

They sprint back to the truck, and of course it won't start. One of them jumps out, grabs a wrench from the toolbox, pulls the intake, sprays in some ether and gets it back on, and it fires up and they peel out.
It's a turbocharged Ford diesel that normally does seventy or eighty, and it won't go past about fifty-five. The passenger looks back, and the thing is still behind them, keeping pace.

They make the last mile to the trailer, run inside, lock the door and cover every window with blankets. Just as the last blanket goes up, something starts tugging at the door. One of them holds it shut, and then the lock starts turning by itself. They tie it in place with a bootlace, grab a hammer, and wait.
A minute later a text comes in from a girl one of them likes, a girl who never texts back. She says she's in trouble and needs them to come get her right now.
They're halfway out the door when they ask if she's got money for diesel, and she writes back asking why she'd want to see them. They haven't talked in months. She never sent that first message.
So they stay inside. Later that night, voices they almost recognize call their names from outside. Neither of them looks.

In the morning there's nothing. No scratches on the trailer, no dents, no prints. Over the next few days they put a salt line around the trailer, stop giving the thing their attention, and pray, and they go over to the reservation to ask for help, without much luck. By the fifth night, the knocking and the scratching have stopped.

Gifford Pinchot National Forest, outside Carson, Washington. A camper and a boyfriend have their tent pitched with the car about a hundred and fifty yards up the hill, and off to the south, somewhere in the thick forest, there's a loud creek they can hear but never actually find.

Around nine, sitting by the fire, they realize they've left something in the car, so he heads up the hill to grab it. While he's gone, knocking starts up in the trees, wood on trunks, maybe four knocks from three different directions, one of them the way he just walked. Then, faintly, from what sounds like the far side of that creek, comes something like a woman screaming. The camper decides it's the forest playing tricks.
He comes back, they crawl into the tent, and within five minutes they hear what they take for an owl.

Except it's no owl they've ever heard. The camper grew up studying zoology and can pick out plenty of exotic calls, and this one is guttural and whooping instead of hooting, and it reminds them of a gibbon.

Then a second voice joins in, and a third, and maybe more. The calls build and build into a loud mess of whoops and howls and noises they still can't describe, and the two of them lie side by side, frozen, as mesmerized as they are scared.
It goes on for several minutes, though they lose track of time, and it ends in a big swelling crescendo that sounds almost like singing. Then it fades away.
And then something comes right up to the tent.

It starts making a rapid chattering sound, and going by where it's coming from, the camper figures it's about seven feet off the ground. It chatters for maybe thirty seconds, right there on the other side of the tent wall, and then it moves off.
Somehow the boyfriend falls asleep. The camper lies awake a while longer, listening to a few more whoops out in the dark, each one further away than the last.
They'd shown up not caring one way or the other about Sasquatch. They both went home believers.

A married couple who hike Appalachia on weekends have had enough strange things happen in the woods over the years that they've come up with two code words. One means 'I think I saw something, but we don't need to leave.' The other means 'I'm looking right at something and we need to go, now.'

It's a rainy Sunday in June, five in the afternoon, and they've got the Fiery Gizzard Trail up on the Cumberland Plateau near Monteagle, Tennessee, all to themselves. About a mile in they start finding clusters of red-capped mushrooms and follow them a little way off the trail toward a meadow, and just before the meadow they pass a stump with broken clay pottery sitting on top of it.

The hiker is walking a little ahead when something very dark brown darts across to the right of the path. It's quick enough that it could be a deer or a coyote, but the hiker says the first code word anyway.
The husband comes up alongside, and the woods go silent. Then there's a sound like a whistle.
His eyes go wide, and he says the second code word.
Right where the movement was, there's a very tall, muscular, dark figure standing on two legs, staring at them. And it doesn't look like Bigfoot.

They turn and speed-walk back toward the trail, and that's when a deep, pulsing hum fills both their ears, so piercing it hurts. They're dizzy and lost, like they're not on the trail even though they know they are, their muscles go weak and they both feel sick, and the hiker keeps silently repeating the name of Jesus just to stay steady.
The whole way back to the car, something is brushing through the trees alongside them. At one point, in full daylight, they see its eyes, and they're glowing.

Back on the road, with their heads and ears still full of pressure, they pass what looks like a deer standing beside the woods. It isn't hurt, but it's wrong. Its legs are twisted the wrong way, its jaw is too big, and it's standing there in an awkward pose, not moving a hair.

Grandma's place is deep in the backwoods near a big national park, up a gravel road so washed out you need a decent vehicle to make it. The cousins live with their moms in a trailer just below her, and the people around there know about the strange sounds and strange animals and strange disappearances around that park.

One night Grandma's in the hospital with an aunt, so the oldest cousin is left in charge of the kids. He's the one they all look up to, the kind of older cousin who'll mess with you but actually cares. They've played all day, and when it gets dark they grab flashlights for manhunt, and the youngest cousin, as always, is the one being hunted.

The youngest runs deep into the woods on the far side of the property and hides behind a log, but gets spotted, and then everybody's running, all the way to the very back of the property line, almost a mile from the house.
And that's where they run into the oldest cousin.
He looks at them, and he sort of growls.
They figure he's joined the game, so they all take off from him, back out onto the gravel road. Behind them he walks out of the tree line in a strange way, almost like he's gloating.

The kids race into the house and start barricading the door to prank him. They've got a few things piled against it and they're noisily dragging the big coffee table over when the oldest cousin walks into the living room.
From the master bedroom. Rubbing his eyes.
All that noise woke him up, and he's mad. Then they tell him about him chasing them through the woods, and his eyes go wide. He sends them all to the bedroom and tells them to stay there.
About twenty minutes later he comes in and tells them not to worry, it was just him, trying to scare them. So they let it go, and get on with the night.

About three years later, when the youngest is thirteen, he finally tells the truth. It wasn't him out there. It was a skinwalker, he said, and he'd had his own run-in with it when he was the same age they'd been that night.

It's a weekday morning in late summer 2019, and a guy and his girlfriend are hiking the Loma Prieta Grade trail in the Forest of Nisene Marks, in the Santa Cruz Mountains. He's spent his whole life in these mountains, and Bigfoot is the last thing on his mind. He's spent most of the hike complaining about his manager.

About an hour in she needs a bathroom break, so they find a gap in the trees and go twenty or thirty feet in, out of sight of the trail. He tosses her the backpack with the toilet paper, she ducks behind a tree, and he walks halfway back to keep watch.
With nothing to do but look around, he catches some movement on his left.
About ten feet away, wrapped around the trunk of a tree, is a hand. It's very dark and very clear. His first thought is somebody in black gloves, maybe some creep peeking at his girlfriend.
Then a face leans out from behind the tree.

He's six foot two, and this thing is seven or eight feet tall. He only ever sees half of it, big black eyes, a broad flat nose, dark skin, blackish-grey hair, and a hint of a peak to the skull. And for no reason he can explain, he's sure it's female.

It leans out twice. It's the eyes he remembers most, mesmerizing, like they're looking right through him, and everything slows down the way it does in a car accident. The whole time, he's aware of two things at once, that face behind the tree and the sound of his girlfriend peeing a few yards away.
The second time it holds his gaze for a few seconds, then pulls back behind the tree and seems to sink down, like it's crouching or lying down. And that's the last he sees of it.
The fear doesn't hit until his girlfriend walks back to him. He grabs her hand, pulls her out to the trail and says they have to go, right now, and they walk down a lot faster than they came up.
She believes him right away. She actually wants to go back and look for it.
He does not.

It's getting dark on an empty back road outside a small Montana town, and two buddies are crawling along with the high beams on, scanning the ditches. One of them lost his phone out here a few days ago when he stopped to take a leak and tumbled into the ditch (as you do), and they've driven thirty miles out looking for it and turned back as the sun went down.
About fifteen miles from town, thirty or forty yards ahead, something huge is crossing the road.

Our witness's brain runs down the list. An elk's most likely, but it doesn't move like an elk. A moose moves in that gangly way, but they're rare around there. It moves a bit like a bear, but it's way too big for a black bear, and grizzlies are almost unheard of in that part of the state. Still, he figures this is going to be a pretty cool sighting.
Then it reaches the edge of the road, stands up on two legs, and walks down into the ditch the way a person would.
He's seen bears walk upright, and it looks awkward and unnatural on them. This is smooth and easy, like it's just how the thing moves.

It climbs the far side of the ditch and steps over a barbed-wire fence four and a half to five feet high, as casually as you'd step over a little garden fence. And as it crosses, it turns its head and looks back at them, and in the headlights they see its profile clearly. It looks like a wolf's head, only two or three times the size.
The arms are way too long for a bear and not as bulky, and he's sure there are long fingers ending in claws. Then it's gone into the dark beyond the fence.

His buddy turns and asks if he saw that. Our witness makes him describe it first, and it matches almost detail for detail. So what does he think it was? The buddy gives a nervous laugh and says "werewolf," the exact word already sitting in our witness's head.
The strange thing is, he wasn't scared, not then and not later. When it looked back at them it just seemed curious, like it was going about its business. He hopes he sees it again.

Washington County, Pennsylvania, two in the morning, at the end of a long gravel road beside a creek. There's one worker out here on the night shift at a water pump station for the fracking sites, with a light plant, a roaring compressor, a spotlight, a porta-potty, and a truck with a flat tire that still runs. No cell signal, and the nearest coworker is a mile up the hill.
Then the frack shuts down, and the pumps go quiet.

And in that silence, about thirty yards in front of the truck, something starts cracking and crashing around in the trees. The worker swings the spotlight over the tree line and there's nothing there.

Then a roar comes out of those trees, louder than anything the worker has ever heard. You can feel it in your ribs, and the truck's mirrors are shaking the whole time it goes on. A big log comes sailing out of the woods and smacks into the front of the truck, and then something crashes off into the dark.

The worker was so scared it was nearly enough to throw up. The coworker up the hill had heard that roar too, a mile away, and came down, and for the rest of the night the two of them made every trip to the pumps together. The worker never took that station alone again.

Later on another crew told the rest. They'd been hearing noises and crashing in those woods for nights, so they pointed the light plant's four big lamps at the tree line after dark. Not long after, during a shift change that left the site empty for half an hour or so, somebody or something shoved that light plant into the creek and wrecked it. And it kept happening like that. Every time anyone pointed a light into those woods, something happened.

A week or two after the job ended, a friend the worker has trusted for years drove down alone after sundown to pick up some equipment. He'd spent plenty of nights alone in the woods and never thought twice, but the minute he stepped out of the truck he felt watched, like he shouldn't be there.
He hooked the equipment up anyway. And as he drove out past the tree line, there was a huge, hulking black figure standing about four feet from his window, watching him go by.

Winter 2023, heavily wooded country in Wisconsin, snow on the ground. Two cousins are still up at two in the morning, playing a video game in the younger one's room while the rest of the house sleeps.
Outside, the porch light is on a motion sensor, and it clicks on. Probably an animal. There's a raccoon that keeps raiding the cat food box, so nobody thinks twice. Then it clicks on again.
When they finally shut the game off to sleep, the light's still on, which means whatever set it off is still out there, moving around.
So they go to the window. At first there's nothing. Then the cousin elbows our witness and swears under his breath.

Further out, past the porch, there's an animal standing there. It's tall, almost as tall as a person, maybe taller, and its eyes are so reflective they look like they're glowing orange. And it's looking straight at them through the glass. It looked like it could see us.
Coyote, is the first thought. But it's way too big, and it doesn't look like any coyote either of them has ever seen.
Eventually it moves off, and after a while the porch light times out and goes dark. The room has no curtains, so they hang a towel over the window before they even try to sleep.
In the morning the aunt and uncle say they saw the light on in the night and figured it was the kids or the raccoon. Probably a coyote, they say, when they hear the rest.

But outside there are huge footprints in the snow. It's been melting all night and all morning, so the tracks aren't crisp enough to make out properly. They're just big. And nobody in that house can say what made them.
It was years before the cousins learned the word dogman, and the description fit.

This van camper has lived on the east side of the Sierra Nevada nearly their whole life, and lives in a van now, parked well away from people. Black bears have tried to get into that van before, and the move is always the same, bang on the window and yell until the bear gives up.

This night, driving back from Southern California, the van pulls into Lone Ranger Canyon in the Alabama Hills, the bare rocky country below Mount Whitney, around half past midnight. By one o'clock our camper is asleep.

Around two thirty, they half wake up to birds. Lots of birds, singing like it's dawn beside a wooded creek. Except there's no creek out here, and there aren't any trees. Confused and tired, they try to go back to sleep, and then the birdsong seems to turn into crickets, really loud crickets, and there weren't any crickets when they pulled in.
They've barely had that thought when something leans against the side of the van.

A deafening wail starts up, part screech and part whistle, and the whole van begins to shake, violently. It's nothing like the slow sway when friends rocked it as a prank a while back. If it's an earthquake, it's bigger than any they've felt in a lifetime in California.

They want to bang on the window and scream at it to stop, like with a bear, but they can't move. Instead they start sobbing, out of nowhere, uncontrollably, in a voice that doesn't even sound like their own. The terror seems to come from outside them, filling the air, heavy, pressing down, and they're sure they're going to die.
It goes on for what feels like minutes.
Then the shaking stops, and so does everything else. No crickets, no birds, just dead silence, and somehow the silence is worse.

It's ten minutes before they can make themselves move. Then they get dressed, grab a long trowel and a flashlight, and step out to look. No bear prints. No fresh footprints. No fresh tire marks, and they'd have heard a vehicle leave.

So they drive out fast, and the dread follows them all the way down Whitney Portal Road and through Lone Pine, and it doesn't lift until they're heading south on the highway. When they finally get signal, there's no earthquake on record for the area.
And for somebody who usually goes out of their way to avoid people, pulling into a rest stop full of sleeping strangers felt like being rescued.

October 2012, near Cayuga, Ontario, about thirty miles south of Hamilton. Our witness works in commercial real estate, and the last stop of the day is an old farmstead at the end of a dead-end country road, hidden at the top of a long driveway, empty since the 1990s.

It's around five thirty when they pull in and start walking the property. The house is boarded up tight. The garage is mostly still standing, but the side door is half broken in, still held by a padlock and two hinges, with the bottom forced inward.
And the door, and the siding all around it, is covered in scratches.

Not dog scratches. Huge, deep, parallel gouges, spaced wide apart like fingernails, made with a lot of force. The ground around the door is covered in paw prints, not round like a dog's but stretched out a bit, and at least five inches across. Our witness sets a size-ten boot over one and the print still shows on both sides.
That's when they notice the woods have gone completely silent.

And the smell hits, wet dog and urine and rot, like a swamp only much worse. All at once they know they're not alone out there, so they head straight back to the car, and something big crashes through the bushes nearby, moving fast and hard.

Doors locked. Engine on. And when the headlights come up, two eyes shine back out of the trees ahead, four or five feet off the ground or higher. Way too high for a dog. In the dusk there might be a big shape back there in the shadows.

Watching it instead of where they're going, they back straight into a marshy patch and get stuck, and it's several frantic seconds of rocking before the car pulls free. When they look up again, it's gone. They drive out of there a lot faster than they came in.
A coworker says bear. But there aren't any wild bears that far south in Ontario.

Later on our witness is handling a farmland sale near Six Nations of the Grand River for an elderly client, a man in his eighties, and asks if he's ever heard of anything strange around there, and mentions the old farm.
He answers with a question. "You seen it, didn't you?"
He won't say much more than that. Only that there are a lot of things unknown to this world, and there was a good reason that place had sat empty for decades.
October 2020, Willow Creek, up in Humboldt County. A farm worker who's been picking up seasonal work around there since July goes on a dinner date with another farm worker from just down the road.

After dinner the two of them drive out to a pull-off on a rocky beach on the Trinity River, planning to lie out under the stars. Then it rains, probably the first rain of the season, so they wait it out in the car for an hour, and when it stops they decide to just sleep right there. They fold the seats down into a bed and set their gear and a guitar out on the gravel.
It's about quarter to midnight. They're sitting in the back with the hatch open, facing the river, wrapped in blankets. The fog is thick, and there isn't a light anywhere.
And from down on the rocks by the water comes a low, guttural growl.

It goes on for about thirty seconds. At first it almost sounds like a didgeridoo, but it's a voice, a gargling growl, and a wave of fear hits them both at the same time. Tears are running down the farm worker's face. "That's not human."
The date yells out into the dark, "Hey, what are you doing down there?"
The growl stops, for about a second. Then whatever it is screams, a sound neither of them ever imagined hearing.

They slam the hatch and lie there shaking, and the sounds get louder, and then there seem to be more than one. High voices and low voices, howling and yelling and sometimes almost laughing, like a cross between a gorilla and a hyena. Then they're all around the car. The voices seem to go back and forth like they're talking to each other, and there are loud thuds they can't place, and the whole thing feels like taunting.
Five minutes of that, maybe, though it feels like forever. And then one of them is right at the rear passenger window, and they both scream.

The date yells, "Drive!" and the farm worker digs the keys out of the blankets and scrambles into the driver's seat, shaking so badly it's hard to work the pedal, and pulls away. The headlights come on, and they never see a thing.

In the morning they drive back out, expecting everything to be gone. Nothing's been touched. The gear, the guitar, the cooler, the beer, all still sitting right where they left it on the gravel, and there's not one track.

There's a big historic park sprawled across the corner where Pennsylvania, Maryland and Delaware meet, about 3,500 acres of thick woods and creeks, and one couple loves to hike it at night. Same half-mile loop from the same old church with a Revolutionary War cemetery, thousands of times, and never once a bad feeling. And our witness is a self-described skeptic.

One Wednesday in August 2023 they head out on a whim around 10:45, and for once they take the narrow gravel road in instead of the paved one. Halfway along, coming around a bend, something shoots across the road through their headlights.
It's somewhere between a dog and a person in size, so fast it almost seems to fly, a black blur with fuzzy details and bright silver eyes. They talk themselves out of it and agree not to dwell on it.

On the trail the frogs and cicadas are deafening, louder than they've ever heard them, so loud they have to raise their voices. But the further they go, the quieter the bugs get. And without saying a word about it, the partner has started hearing what sound like very distant voices.
About a quarter mile in, a sharp, crackling sound cuts through the air, like a glitching microphone or megaphone somewhere far off, in woods with nothing out there for an echo to bounce off.

Our skeptic stops dead and asks if he heard it. He did, and he admits he's been telling himself he was imagining the voices the whole time. They turn around without a word and walk fast back to the car, sure the whole way that something is following them.

At the first turn on the drive out, on a road they've driven thousands of times, the skeptic suddenly has no idea which way to go. Then the partner says, "Do you not know where you are right now? Because neither do I."
They guess right. The next road runs along the edge of the park, and it's full of fog that wasn't there an hour ago.

And just as they pass the stretch where they turned back on the trail, the animal crosses in front of them again. Closer this time, and clearer. The same silver eyes, what look like ears or horns, and impossibly fast.
Even now, just talking about it gives them a burning in their sinuses, watering eyes and a tingle at the back of the skull.

It's 2015, on a small cattle ranch near Marlin, Texas, rolling grassland and thick oak woods with a creek running along the bottom, and on days off the ranch hand likes to paddle a kayak upstream to the gravel bars full of arrowheads and fossils.

About fifteen minutes into one trip there are two deer on the bank. Deer never know what to make of a kayak, so the ranch hand paddles slowly toward them and the pair just stand there watching. Then, at about twenty yards, both deer suddenly look back down the creek, snort the way deer do when they smell danger, and take off.
So the ranch hand turns around to see what spooked them.
Seventy-five yards downstream, something hairy and shaped like a person is leaning out over the creek bank, holding onto a big oak branch with one arm so it won't fall in.

It's mid-afternoon and the thing is backlit, so there's no face, just the upper body, and the hair on its arm hangs two or three inches long, black, except where the sun comes through and turns it brown. For six to ten seconds the two of them just stare at each other. Then it pulls itself back behind the tree, and it's gone.

Later the ranch hand paddles back to that tree. The brush that hid its lower half is about three feet tall, which puts it at a little over six feet. There's no track in the hard grey clay and no hair on the bark or the briars.

Back at the house the boss, a retiree from Connecticut, is skeptical, but she mentions something odd. For several days now the cows have stopped sleeping in the pasture by the creek. They've been bedding down by the barn, about as far from the water as they can get.

A month later the ranch hand is up in a tree stand over a corn feeder at the edge of the creek woods, waiting on hogs that usually show up by eight. Nothing comes. Then around nine, just as it gets too dark to see through the scope, something pushes through the brush behind the stand like a group of hogs, and stops dead twenty yards away.
Except hogs grunt as they come in. This doesn't make a sound.
When the ranch hand climbs down a few minutes later, it's gone, just as quietly. And for a few seconds a faint musky, rotten-egg smell drifts by on the breeze.

It's late July, under a full moon, and five friends are walking the last mile into the woods outside Council Hill, Illinois, looking for an old farmhouse that local legend says is haunted. A metal bar across a bridge stopped the car, so they're on foot now, and the night already feels off.

It's weirdly cold for July. The fields on one side of the road are full of fireflies, and the side toward the house doesn't have a single one. They're tired and short of breath, their phone and flashlight batteries are draining fast, and howls and screams carry in from somewhere off in the distance. Coyotes, they tell themselves. Rabbits and other little animals keep running past them, all of them heading away from the house.
For the last hundred and fifty yards they all feel watched from a thick tangle of brush on the left.

They scramble up a gravel embankment onto a railway bridge to get a look at the house, and while the other four stay there admiring it in the moonlight, he walks about a hundred yards down the tracks on his own.

Up ahead, a shadow moves around a railway signal light and blocks it out for a few seconds. He still isn't scared, so he creeps ten steps closer, and that's when he sees something crouched on the embankment beside the tracks.
Then it stands up, with a sound like knuckles cracking into a microphone, and steps into the light.

It's six or seven feet tall and grey, with huge muscled shoulders and a thick ruff of fur around the neck. The head is exactly a wolf's, with glowing white eyes and teeth showing at the sides of the mouth. The forearms are freakishly long, the huge hands end in black claws, and the lower legs bend backward like a dog's.
It takes three steps and breaks into a hunched trot, arms hanging limp, longer than its lower legs.

He screams at the others to run. Three of them take off down the tracks, and he and one other friend dive down the embankment into the brush. At the old railway underpass a light suddenly appears and floats toward the two of them, then stops a few feet away, with no voices and no engine, and when they creep through to look there's nothing there for three hundred yards.
They find the others by their shouting. One is white as a sheet, and the youngest is in shock, staring at nothing and muttering one word, over and over.
Werewolf.

Way out in southern Ohio, about as far from anything as you can get in that state, an older man lives alone in an old farmhouse on a big piece of land, and he loves driving his golf cart along the trails through his woods. Two friends come by a couple of times a month to clear fallen trees off those trails for him.

Then one visit he tells them he's stopped going out on the cart, because he's scared. Way at the back of the property there's an old one-room schoolhouse, abandoned for decades, windows boarded up and half the roof caved in. Somebody's living in it, he says. He's seen a man dressed all in black hiding behind the trees near it, and the boards over the doorway have been torn off.
The two of them offer to go take a look. One of them figures the board just rotted off and the old man mistook a shadow for a person.

By the time they've walked the half mile back to it, it's nearly dark. And something has definitely been using the place. Saplings are pushed over, there's a trail worn through the weeds, and the boards have been ripped off the door and one window, with broken pieces still lying on the ground.
Then they hear movement inside.

One of them runs to the doorway with the other right behind and shines a flashlight in, and something the size of a big man, covered in long dark hair, shoots across the far side of the room on two legs and steps right out through the open window.

They run around the corner after it. It stops for a second at the edge of the trees and looks back at them, and its eyes throw back a faint orange shine in the flashlight. Then it's gone into the woods, unbelievably fast and almost silent.

These are two experienced outdoorsmen who've watched bears stand up on their hind legs, and this was no bear, and it was too fast to be a person. They don't even believe in Bigfoot, and what they saw doesn't fit anyway. It was slimmer, without the broad shoulders, and its head looked small for its body.

The next day they put up three trail cameras around the schoolhouse. Two of them catch the usual woodland animals. The third has been twisted around its tree to face away from the building, and it didn't take a single picture.

It's 2018, just before sunset, and a woman selling cable door to door is walking alone down a long road on a little peninsula near Cape May, New Jersey. She's spent the day in a small town where people stared at her or turned away, and now her last few addresses are a handful of mostly empty vacation homes on a marshy bay, at the end of a long stretch of woods.
She lingered too long admiring the houses, and the sun is almost down. She's small, she hates being alone in isolated places after dark, and there's no cell signal, so she starts back at a fast walk.

When she hits the wooded stretch, with no streetlights and the light going fast, she notices the woods have gone completely silent. No crickets, no birds. She stops, with a chill running down her spine and the feeling that she's being watched.
Up ahead, something big steps out of the tree line onto the road.
It's dog-shaped, but dogs don't get that big. For a moment it doesn't seem to notice her. Then it does, and it just stands there watching her, like it's deciding what to do with her.

It's too dark to see the face, but she can make out the outline. It's way too big for a black bear, at least five feet at the shoulder on all fours, and hugely muscled, like a wolf on steroids, with a head shaped like a German shepherd's, ears up and a long snout.

Her heart is pounding, and she knows that if it wants her, she can't stop it. She doesn't believe in cryptids, so she tells herself it has to be a big, skittish coyote. And standing still feels more dangerous by the second.
So she lets out the loudest, ugliest scream-howl she can manage, and she runs.

The animal flinches down into a defensive crouch, then seems to decide she isn't worth the trouble, and lopes off into the woods. Not very far, though. She doesn't stop running until she hits the lights of a summer camp, and she collapses onto a picnic table, gasping, watching the tree line.

At her next address the family listens to the whole story, and the mom asks why on earth her company sent her out there alone. These woods are dangerous after dark, she says, and she hints at run-ins of her own that she can't explain.
And they won't let her go back outside.

It's a hot, sticky afternoon in mid-June, halfway up a mountainside in eastern Kentucky, seven miles from the nearest paved road. You only get there by going down a deep holler, following an old creek bed and climbing around two hills, and the slopes are so thick with hemlock and beech they block out the light on a cloudy day.

A carpenter and his great-uncle are clearing trees around a new hunting cabin on family land. This is a man who's spent his whole life in these woods, trapping, digging roots, hunting everything from dove to bear, and in his words he does not believe in haints or goblins.
They shut off their saws to rest and drink some iced tea, and in the quiet, he hears knocking.
It isn't sharp. It's a dull thonk, like a round of poplar bouncing off a woodpile, or a mallet on the end of a seasoned board. Thonk, thonk, thonk, thonk. He knows woodpeckers, and this isn't one.
He looks at his uncle, and right as their eyes meet it comes again, closer. And then an answering set of knocks comes from further up the mountain.

He figures it's trespassers, two of them, and that makes him mad, so he grabs a chunk of wood, smacks the nearest tree as hard as he can, and stares across the holler to where the first knocks came from.

That's when he sees it. More than a hundred yards off, beside a maple in the tall mountain laurel, there's a jet-black shape, with a reddish tinge at the tips of the hair where the sun hits it. Half a shoulder, part of a chest, the top of a belly. No head, no arms or legs. It isn't a bear, it isn't an elk, and it isn't a shadow.
His blood runs cold. He keeps asking his uncle what it is, but he can't tear his eyes away long enough to look over. Then it shifts a little, and it's gone.
When he finally turns around, his uncle is sitting there calm as anything. The old man says, "Hmm," stands up, starts his saw and goes back to work.
Years later a cousin mentions camping on that same creek with the uncle back in the 1980s, and seeing something big cross the trail way up ahead.
The uncle has never once acknowledged what happened that afternoon, no matter how many times he's been asked.

It's opening week of deer season, November 2013, on family hunting land near Cedarville in Michigan's eastern Upper Peninsula. There's a big front yard and a gravel driveway, and deep hardwood forest on every side. She grew up hunting up here, and her husband's a city kid.
Around eleven at night they go out for a smoke, and they bring the rifle like always, because of bears. She stays up on the porch. He goes down the steps into the yard and stands there facing her.
Then footsteps start coming up the dark driveway.

Slow and heavy, like a really big man walking, but heavier than anything she's ever heard in the woods, full-grown bears included. And with them comes a strange, heavy breathing. Nothing she knows sounds like that, and that alone scares her.
Then it steps out of the tree line at the edge of the yard, right behind her husband.

It's on two legs, at least seven feet tall and maybe four hundred pounds, with fur so black it looks darker than the night around it. It paces along the edge of the yard but won't step into the porch light, so she can barely make out its body. What she can see is a head like a wolf's, with a snout and tall pointed ears standing straight up, and instead of front legs, very long arms that end in hands.
She grabs the rifle and starts shooting and screams at her husband to get up on the porch. He runs up, takes the rifle, tells her to find a weapon and hide.

So she locks herself in a bedroom closet with a big knife and listens to him out there shooting and reloading for about ten minutes. While it paces, he says, it sometimes drops to all fours. And when it finally takes off, it runs upright like a man, impossibly fast, slipping through the brush instead of crashing through it.
She stays in that closet till sunrise. In daylight there's no blood, no hair and no tracks, though those footsteps felt heavy enough to shake the ground.

Later a neighbour she's known since high school tells them he's seen it too, the winter before. There was a party at his cabin, and he heard heavy steps on the porch, and he pulled back the curtain, and there it was on the other side of the door glass, looking down at him.
Only that time, with snow on the ground, its fur was white.

This one comes from a moose hunt in Maine. Our witness's dad had drawn a permit, and the guide was a nurse he works with at the local ER, a man in his forties who's been guiding since he was twenty and has spent his whole life in those woods. So of course the question came up. Had he ever run into anything strange out there? Once, he said, about twenty years ago. But first he made a point of saying he's never believed in any of it, and he wouldn't claim it was Bigfoot.

He was guiding a bear hunt. The way it works, you set out bait barrels full of sweet stuff and put each hunter up in a tree stand where he can see one. At the end of the day he heads off on foot through the woods to pick up his hunter.
He's halfway there when an enormous WOOP rings out through the trees.
Then another, and another, and in a whole life in those woods he has never heard anything like it. He's terrified.
He keeps walking. And now he can clearly hear footsteps behind him. It's too dark to see a thing, so he walks the rest of the way with his pistol out.
Then there's a loud crash out in the dark, like something got thrown, maybe a log, or like a dead tree being shoved over.
When he gets to the stand, his hunter is shaking. He'd been hearing those whoops too, and for more than half an hour something had been walking around behind his stand.
Neither of them hung around to find out what it was. They got out of there fast.

That's the whole story. He never saw a thing, and he still won't say what it was. But he told it quietly, and sincerely, even with Dad cracking jokes. And his stretch of woods happens to be the same part of Maine where, back in 1886, the local papers reported that a ten-foot wild man had been killed.

Summer, at a family cabin on Long Lake near Danbury, up in the forests of northwestern Wisconsin. He's sixteen or seventeen, six foot four, a hunter and a camper and a martial artist, and by his own admission a cocky kid who thinks he's invincible.

One hot afternoon he and his cousin play airsoft. He's taking it seriously, full woodland camo and a mask, and his cousin's in jeans and a T-shirt. He leads the game into the woods, where he feels at home, and about a hundred and fifty metres in they stop. Just to mess with his cousin, he shushes him and whispers that they're being watched.
It wasn't much of a joke, he says.

Because the second he says it, he notices the woods have gone dead silent, and in his experience that means a big predator is close. Then the feeling of being watched hits him for real. He starts scanning the trees, and what gives it away is a glint of teeth, whitish teeth.

At the edge of a clearing about forty metres away, something is crouched down, holding onto a tree with its left hand. It's panting. Its ears are up, it has reddish-brown fur and a canine look to it, and it's watching them. The only word that comes into his head is werewolf.
He tells his cousin they have to go, and his cousin bolts.

He's still got his eyes on it when his cousin starts running, and in that instant it charges. It comes at them on two legs for maybe ten feet, then drops down onto all fours, and he turns and sprints. The whole way out of those woods he can hear it crashing through the undergrowth behind them.
Back at the cabin he told his cousin it must have been a bear, so he wouldn't be scared, and he's still not sure his cousin ever actually saw it. But he knows bears, and it wasn't one.
That cocky kid who thought he was invincible doesn't go into the woods alone anymore if he can help it, and when he has to, he goes armed.

Back in the 80s and early 90s he was deep in the California hardcore punk scene, and on weekends when there wasn't a show, he'd load his Toyota pickup with a bike, fishing gear and a sidearm and head up into the Sierra Nevada alone. He wasn't looking for anything in particular. Just some kind of connection, with life, or the universe.

One October, when he's about thirty, he drives up to Rock Creek after work on a Friday, two weeks before the campground closes for winter. The only other people there are an older couple and the old ranger who knows him from all his visits.
Saturday is perfect, a long bike ride, some fishing, dinner, and he's in bed by ten in the back of the truck under the shell. It's bitterly cold.
Sometime in the night he wakes up, and as he's drifting off again he hears a big rig braking on the curves of the highway above camp, which he's used to.
And then he hears something he isn't used to.
A whoop. It isn't close, and it doesn't last long, but it sticks with him. He tells himself it has to be an owl, and the rest of the weekend goes by with nothing else.

Years later he's eating dinner in front of the TV when a wilderness survival show comes on. The host is alone in the mountains, hears a strange call in the dark, and is clearly rattled. They play the call over and over, and the hair on his arms stands up, because it's the sound from Rock Creek, note for note.
He finds himself crying, and not from sadness, and he still isn't sure why. He'd heard a Bigfoot and didn't know it for twenty years.

Then he starts thinking about all those years alone up there, and a couple of other times when a wave of dread hit him for no reason he could see and he just bolted. Once he left in such a hurry he tripped on a rock and went face first into a puddle before scrambling back to the truck. He'd always put it down to imagination, or gut instinct, or maybe a bad spirit. He never went back to those spots.
That TV show ended his love affair with the mountains. He has no wish to see or hear one of those things ever again.

Summer of 2015, a small one-storey ranch house outside a Montana town of about two thousand people, nearest neighbour a mile away, and a man living there alone. Right from the start he understood why the previous owners left in such a hurry.

At night the woods behind the house are full of screams and growls. He's read that raccoons and bobcats can make some unearthly sounds and tells himself that's all it is, but those woods always feel wrong, like he's being watched.

About two weeks in, a thunderstorm keeps him up, and around two in the morning he gets a glass of water at the kitchen sink, under a little window facing the yard and the tree line. Lightning flashes, and for an instant there it is, a few steps into the yard from the trees.

His first thought is bear, but it's standing on two legs, facing the house. The legs are shaped like a dog's, with that backward-bending hock, with dark fur, and the upper body is massive, arms nearly reaching the ground. He stands frozen, waiting for the next flash. When it comes, the yard is empty.
He buys a gun the next day. Weeks go by with nothing, and then one night his satellite reception keeps cutting out, so he takes the rifle and a flashlight out to fix the dish.
The first thing he notices is the silence. On a summer night those woods are usually alive with sound, and there's nothing.
He's adjusting the dish when a stick snaps to his left. He swings the light toward it and meets a pair of eyes, red as blood.

The head looks like a deformed German shepherd's, long snout, pointed ears, and he hates the word, but it looks like a werewolf. Black fur, shaggy in patches, hugely muscled, crouched half in and half out of the trees about twenty feet away. And even crouching, its head is level with his. He's six feet tall.

The rifle never even crosses his mind. He backs away slowly without breaking eye contact, then turns and runs harder than he ever has, and inside he locks every door and window, closes every blind, and sits against the wall holding the gun until morning.
He doesn't live there anymore. "It felt unnatural. It felt evil." It felt like it had been stalking him, playing with him, and he believes it would have killed him.

About thirty-five years ago, a teenage girl is babysitting at the last house on a quiet road outside Port Alberni, on Vancouver Island. Behind the house the forest runs unbroken over a mountain range toward Horne Lake. No streetlights, no motion lights, nothing.

She doesn't scare easily, and part of that is the family dog, a big German shepherd cross and a fantastic guard dog. Whenever his ears go up at a noise outside, she slides open the patio door and he charges off into the dark barking at whatever it is, a raccoon, a stray dog, and a while later he whines at the door to come back in.

So one night his ears go up at something she can't hear, and she goes to let him out like always. The heavy slider sticks about eighteen inches open, and while she wrestles with it he's pushing past her leg to get out. The moon is nearly full, and the yard is bright.
And at the same moment, she and the dog both see it, and they both freeze.

About thirty feet away, beside a stand of trees, a big hairy figure is standing upright. The moon is behind it, so its outline is sharp, and one big arm is resting against the tree next to it. Her mind keeps flipping back and forth. A person, watching her? No, it has to be a bear standing up. Then it shifts a little, she sees its profile, and she knows it's neither.
