But it's the dog that convinces her. He doesn't tear off barking like he always does. He just stands there rigid beside her, every bit as petrified as she is. She tries to make herself move and physically can't, for twenty or thirty seconds that feel like minutes.
Finally she shoves the dog out, slams the slider shut, and hides in a room with no windows.
She never hears him bark. She never hears him crashing off through the brush.
When she finally works up the nerve to cross in front of a window to the phone, she calls her dad, and he comes over. He finds the dog curled up on the front step, not making a sound.
She's seen more than forty bears in her life. She knows what a bear looks like. And her heart still races when she thinks about that night.

There's a road in central Illinois called Cole Hollow Road, and since the 1970s people out there have talked about something big, pale and hairy in the woods. Our newcomer had never heard a word about it before moving in with a friend and the friend's dad, in a house at the end of a long dirt driveway deep in the forest off that road.
The friend and his dad were full of stories, sightings from fifty years back, trash cans with dents shaped like fists. The newcomer didn't buy any of it.

Within days, stuff started happening. Several times that first week the newcomer stepped out the front door to find the trash can flung across the big yard, the garbage torn open and scattered, and the can dented like it had been punched.

The newcomer's room is in the basement, with a little covered porch and a sliding door a few feet from a wooded ditch. A couple of weeks in, six friends are sitting out on that porch talking late when small rocks start coming at them out of the ditch. Most of the group figure it's a prank and throw rocks back, and more rocks come. Something feels wrong to the newcomer, who talks everybody into going inside.
Nothing else happens, so around two in the morning they all go back out. There are tall, leafy plants all around the porch, thick enough to screen it, but with gaps you can see through.
One friend is up in a tall chair telling a story, and everybody's laughing and cutting in, and under all that noise the newcomer hears what sounds like heavy footsteps, close by.
Then, through the gaps in the leaves right behind that friend's head, there's a patch of shaggy, pure white fur.
The newcomer freezes, then goes into a full-on panic attack, and the others get everybody inside. On the way there's one glance back, and the gaps in the leaves are empty.
The newcomer never slept in that basement again, and moved out as soon as it could be managed.

He's worked at the same fenced federal installation since 2009, and every morning he gets there around five, in the dark, no matter the season. There's a fence over six feet high with barbed wire angled out along the top, and a herd of about two dozen deer that lives on the property. In all those years he's never once driven in without seeing some of them.
One morning in the spring of 2025, walking in from the parking lot, he notices it's dead silent. No birds, no spring peepers, no crickets, nothing.

Half an hour later his boss pulls in and stops where she always does, about twenty-five feet from the fence, to light a cigarette. It's still silent, she said, and then something hit that fence with a bang, like a baseball thrown as hard as you can throw it. The lot lights let you see more than a hundred feet down the fence both ways, and nothing was moving.
The next morning, walking in, he hears something pacing along the outside of the fence, just inside the tree line. And it sounds like it's on two legs. So on a whim he calls out, Hello, good morning!
The footsteps stop.

Then there are weeks of silent mornings. In early July, as he turns into the lot, his headlights sweep across the big drainage pond past it, and five or six feet down the embankment there's a tall, slender, chocolate-brown figure standing there, watching three deer at the far end of the water. It's built like a teenage boy right after his last growth spurt, all long and lanky, and from the lot he figures it's seven feet tall.
It doesn't wait for him to park. By the time he hurries over there's nothing to see or hear, and the deer are gone too.

That afternoon he goes back in the sun. Halfway down the embankment there's a flattened patch in the tall grass about four feet across, with no trail in and no trail out, and deer always leave a trail. And the spot sits lower on the slope than he thought, which means whatever stood there was a lot taller than seven feet.
Since that morning the deer have all but vanished. The crickets and the peepers came back, but the morning birds never did.
He says hello every morning now when he walks in.
Northeastern Pennsylvania, around 2019. A scientist and a friend are hiking a wooded mountain above a reservoir. It isn't truly remote out there, but there's plenty of forest.

Before they left, the friend's dad, whose family has been in those parts for generations, told them to be careful. There are a lot of old abandoned four-wheeler trails up there, he said, and he hinted there were things in those woods to watch out for.
So of course they get lost. They wander onto those old ATV trails, and the sun starts going down, and they're stressed and hurrying when they hear something moving and turn around.
Long reddish-brown hair sweeps right past them at eye level.
It's so long that the scientist's first confused thought is a woman's hair, and the scientist actually asks if that's the friend's mom, out looking for them because they're late.
The friend says no. That's not a person. Look down.

They're standing right at the edge of a steep slope, and whatever just passed them is walking on the ground below. For its hair to be at their eye level, it has to be three or four feet taller than they are. It doesn't run, but its strides are so long and so quick that it's there and gone in a second. No clothes, just all that reddish-brown hair and an earthy, nasty smell.

The fear hits them both at once. They ditch the trails completely and run straight downhill through the trees, and they come out way further around the reservoir than they should have, and they make it back to the car.
When they tell the friend's dad, he isn't surprised at all. All his friends know those animals live up there, he says, and people stay out of that area to leave them be.
Everybody the scientist has told since says the same thing. Obviously a bear. But the bears around there are small and black, and what walked past them below was neither a bear nor a person.

It's half past two on a clear night in May 2021, a few miles east of Hope, BC, and a freight train coming back from Boston Bar has just gone into emergency braking. It hasn't derailed, and the engineer gets the air pressure back, but they've lost contact with the monitoring unit at the very end of the train, and somebody has to walk back there and reset it.

That job falls to the conductor. He grabs bear spray, a knife, flares and one of the railway's old lanterns, the kind with a little bulb that reaches about a hundred feet on a fresh battery, and he starts walking. The train is almost 12,000 feet long, more than two miles of it.
He makes it to the end, hits the button, gets the communication back and starts the long walk back to the front.

Partway there, he sees one of the cars up ahead swaying side to side. His first thought is a rockslide, rocks hitting the train and maybe more coming down on him. Then as he gets closer he sees something under the car, and he figures it's a bear. So he stops about two car lengths back, gets the bear spray ready, and plans to climb the nearest car if it comes at him.
It comes out from under the car. And it stands up.

In the lantern light it's on two feet, almost as tall as the railcar, black, he thinks, and it's definitely no bear. The closest thing he can come up with is Andre the Giant, only a lot bigger. Its eyes are shining in the lantern beam.
They stare at each other for what feels like forever, probably five to seven seconds. Then it turns and walks off up the hillside on two legs, and it never makes a sound.
He was so scared he wet himself a little and cried, because he was sure he was about to die. He ran most of the way back to the locomotive and felt watched the entire time.

When the engineer asked why he was so out of breath, he joked that a big cat must've been chasing him, and he never told the engineer the truth. He doesn't do road trips anymore. He only works in the rail yard now.

It's a hot, sticky midsummer afternoon in the North Carolina foothills, one or two o'clock, and a man is sitting on an upturned bucket on his own wooded land, packing cob, that mix of clay and straw, into the gaps between the logs of the cabin he's building. His brother and a friend are supposed to show up to help.
All of a sudden he gets the feeling he's being watched. He figures it's those two trying to sneak up on him for a laugh, so he keeps working and pretends not to notice.
Then off to his left he hears leaves crunching, light and slow, getting closer. Deer wander through all the time, so he's not worried. But when he turns his head toward the sound, it stops.

So he stands up and looks. Years ago he cut a narrow lane through the brush there for deer hunting, and at the edge of it, twenty or thirty feet away and half hidden in the leaves, is what looks like a person covered head to toe in fur. He can see a very broad, long shoulder and arm, and a light brown face with some hair on it, looking right back at him.
They look at each other for ten or fifteen seconds.
Still thinking it's a person, he says, "Hello."
It shifts its weight, turns its shoulder toward him, and calmly walks back the way it came.

Now he's annoyed that somebody's trespassing that deep in his woods, so he goes after it. It speeds up. He runs, yelling "Hey, stop!", and he hears it break into a full sprint on two legs. He's a big guy and it's brutally hot, and he gives up pretty quick.

That's when it sinks in. It was about six foot five or six, a little taller than him, with long shaggy fur the colour of a golden retriever, and it looked exactly like somebody in a fur suit. "Why would anyone wear a fur coat in the woods when it's ninety-something degrees out?"
What sticks with him most is how calm it was, like it had just been standing there watching him work, curious about what he was up to.

November, deep in the Ouachita Mountains, and four hikers are camped in a rocky clearing beside a stream, with the slope they just came down behind them and a rock cliff right across the water. One of them is a visitor from Bangladesh who's never been here before. They haven't seen another person all day, and on the way down they passed six or seven uprooted trees stacked into the same triangle shape, which one of them, a trail steward, put down to storms.

Around nine, cooking under a clear sky with no moon, a loud wooden knock comes from the slope behind them. Twenty seconds later another one answers from the cliff across the stream, then another from behind, back and forth for about a minute. Then the woods go dead silent.

They laugh it off and swap Sasquatch stories until half past eleven, when the steward holds up a hand. It's gone silent again. All four of them hear slow, careful footsteps in the dry leaves behind them, a pause, and then something bolts off to the left, and ten seconds later there are three heavy splashes, like something just crossed twenty-five to forty feet of knee-deep water in three strides. Their flashlights show nothing.

They tell themselves it's a black bear and bury the food under rocks away from the tents. Then a clear whoo-OOP comes from the top of the cliff, and another knock, and then fist-sized stones start raining down from up there, four and five at a time, splashing into the stream right in front of them.
The knocking goes on in the distance until they finally fall asleep.
In the morning the visitor is washing clothes in the stream when he hears rustling up on the cliff. There's a black shape looking down at him over the rocks. He freezes, thinking bear, and stands up.
And it stands up too, on two legs, copying him.

Against the bright sky he can't see a face, just a massive body shaped like a man and covered in dark, dirty, matted hair, way bigger than any person. They stare at each other for he doesn't know how long. Then it turns and walks calmly away on two legs, hardly making a sound.

He walks back to camp and says it plain. I just saw a bigfoot. Nobody laughs. They climb up to the spot and it reeks of rotting meat and iron, and the steward, who's about six foot three, barely comes halfway up the rock that thing seemed to fill.
When they go back for their food, the rocks they piled on it and the food underneath are both gone without a trace.

It's a cool day, probably fall, in the Berkshires of western Massachusetts, and two brothers have brought their kids out to the old spot where the family used to camp back in the 70s and 80s. It's a wildlife refuge now, no cars, nice and quiet. One brings his fifteen-year-old son, and the other brings his little girl, about six.
All along the trails there are birds and squirrels and chipmunks everywhere. Then they come out at a pond, and the little girl starts trying to catch frogs.
And everything goes silent, like somebody hit mute. No wind, no birds, nothing.

The hair stands up on the back of one uncle's neck. He's the woodsman of the two, he's run into bears and bobcats without batting an eye, and he looks over at his son, who looks just as rattled and says, Dad, I want to leave.

So he tells his brother quietly that they need to go. His brother hadn't noticed a thing until he was told to listen, and then he agreed. They call the girl away from the water and walk straight back to the car, and the whole way the woodsman feels watched. He's refused to ever go back, and for years the family teased him about it.
Then, five years later, the son pulled a cousin aside, nervous, and said something else happened that day. I saw a Bigfoot.

Coming up to the pond he was trailing a little behind the others, and out of the corner of his eye he caught something dark moving. He turned and saw what he figured was a bear beside a tree at the edge of the woods, so he stopped and watched it. And it wasn't a bear. It looked like a big man covered in hair, crouched down beside that tree.
Then it stood up.
It looked right at him, with eyes he says were red, and then it turned and walked off into the woods.
He kept that to himself for five years, begged his cousin not to tell the family, terrified they'd all make fun of him.

It's 4:30 in the morning, late August 2013, up a holler in West Virginia. He's a first responder, trained to keep his head, and he's just home from the late shift. He flips on the porch light and heads out the back door to dump the cat's litter box into the strip of grass behind the house, grass more than five feet tall, with the family junkyard on the other side and a ridge rising up behind it all.
Off to his left, past the light, he hears a few deer thudding away. He spooks them most nights.

He walks down the twelve steps, bends over and empties the box at the edge of the grass. And as he straightens up, something in the grass right in front of him, no more than seven feet away, stands up at the same time.

He isn't worried. Every month or so he chases scrap thieves out of that junkyard, so he's already putting on his sternest face to start yelling. Then a big dark head rises out of the grass, then shoulders, and it just keeps rising.

The moon's behind it, and it blots out part of the ridge and part of the moon. Eight or nine feet tall, he figures, three times as wide as him, and he can't make out any features, just hair or fur where the moonlight bleeds around its edges.

He freezes, still holding the litter box. In his head he's screaming at himself to run, that it could just reach out and grab him, but his body won't move. He's had three bear encounters, including a bluff charge, and he's never been scared like this.

Then something arm-shaped swings across the top of the grass, and the shape gets narrower. It's four or five steps before he understands it's turned and is walking away from him toward the ridge, on two legs.

When it reaches the bottom of the slope, he runs. Up the steps, inside, litter box still in his hand, hands shaking so hard he can barely work the deadbolt. Only when he tells himself to breathe so he can open the gun safe does he suck in a huge gasp and realize he hasn't taken a breath since he stood up.
He stands ten feet from the back door with his rifle aimed, waves of nausea rolling over him, sure it's coming back.
It never did. He used to think Sasquatch was fun. Now he can't stand anything to do with it.

It's around ten at night at a nature centre in southeastern Wisconsin, and a nineteen-year-old and his date are the only car in the lot. They hike up through the woods to the top of the main hill, where an old wooden bench looks out over the distant lights of Waukesha, and they spread a blanket twenty-five or thirty yards down the far side, out of sight of the bench.
About forty-five minutes later he hears somebody up top, rustling around in the leaves and dirt. And then a huffing, puffing, low growling noise.
He crouches and whispers to her to stay flat and stay still.

Then a figure shows up right where the bench is, and the noises keep going. His first thought is some weird guy standing on the bench. But the moon is bright, and he can see it from the waist up, a thick, solid, dark shape with a head way bigger than any man's. The head keeps snapping side to side while it huffs and puffs, like it's in a frenzy, or like it's scanning the hillside. It never paces. It just stays in one spot, jerking its head around.
He's still telling himself it must be standing on the bench. That would explain the height.

Then it snaps its head to the right one last time, and takes off, and it doesn't jump down off anything. It runs bolt upright at an angle down the side of the hill, thirty or forty yards, faster than any person could, arms tucked at its sides and bent in an L, with almost no swing at all. The huffing stops the second it starts running. And he has the feeling it could've gone even faster.
Then it's gone into the woods.

He grabs the blanket, pulls her to her feet and says they have to go, now. They're about a hundred yards from the car when a screech rings out in the woods behind them, part yelp, and it goes on for ten or fifteen seconds. He's never heard anything like it. She clings to him, they freeze, and then they jog the rest of the way to the car as quietly as they can.
He figures it was over eight feet tall, more than three hundred pounds, one solid colour, and no clothes.
He's never gone back into those woods.

It's a spring weekday high on a mountain in Oregon, an old mining district full of abandoned shafts and crumbling 1800s buildings. A rockhound who's been coming up here for years to collect quartz crystals and gold has brought a roommate along, and there's no sign of another soul in that part of the forest.

They camp in a rough clearing backed by a boulder field and a sheer rock face, with the car about fifty feet from the tent. The car's right there, so what could go wrong? Still, all day long the rockhound can't shake the feeling of being watched, and that's never happened up here before.
Around nine they go to bed. The roommate is out right away. The rockhound is just drifting off when the brush at the tree line starts to shake.
Elk and small animals wander through camp all the time. This sounds big.

Then the shaking stops, and something steps out onto the open ground with a heavy, distinct footfall, and it walks right up to the tent. On two legs. The rockhound lies there rigid, listening to heavy breathing, and then silence.
Then the bushes rattle again, and again something walks up to the tent. And it's never heard walking away.

A sharp elbow wakes the roommate, with a whisper to just listen. He looks at the rockhound like it's all in somebody's head, until the bushes shake and the footsteps come right up to the tent again. His eyes go wide. "Oh my God," he whispers, "that's two feet."

For twenty minutes it keeps happening, steps up to the tent over and over, and never once any steps going away. Then something goes over to the outhouse and shakes it hard. After about forty-five minutes everything goes quiet, and they wait another twenty.

Then they grab the only weapon they've got, a small axe, rip open the tent and sprint for the car. The roommate starts it and hits the headlights, flooding the clearing, and there's nothing there. He jumps out, grabs the whole tent with everything still inside, throws it in the back seat, and they drive down that mountain in pitch dark, waiting the whole way for something to come running out at the car.
The rockhound has been back a few times since, and has had two more strange experiences up there. Both times, the rockhound slept in the car.

Every summer from about 1978 to 1984, a family camped for a week on the west shore of Lake Tahoe, and the dad always tried to get a site in the back loop, the most wooded part, right up against the trailhead into the Desolation Wilderness. Their boy grew up totally comfortable sleeping out under the stars, but whenever he rode his BMX near that trailhead he felt uneasy, and he never knew why.

Over those six summers, things kept happening. Before dawn one morning, rocks and debris came flying sideways into the tent. Another early morning they heard two-legged footsteps circling the tent, close, and when he unzipped the window there was nothing there.

One night around nine they're walking to the lake along a really dark, heavily wooded stretch of bike path, far from the campsites, and something is walking upright in the trees to their right. When they stop, it stops. When they walk, it walks. They never see it.

At one campfire, a girl stands up because she sees red eyeshine about ninety feet out in the dark, and a boy stands up and says he sees it too, and she's so rattled she goes straight back to her family's RV. And once, at check-in, the ranger at the kiosk mentioned they'd been hearing Bigfoot screams at night, and the kid just stared, baffled.

But here's the one he can't shake. One evening he and a buddy prank two girls at the campfire. They take turns slipping off into the dark, picking up a ten- or twenty-pound rock and heaving it into the air so it comes down with a heavy thud, and the girls shriek and laugh until they catch on.
The next morning a boy in their tent says that late in the night he heard a scream 'like a woman being murdered.'
Then the girls come over and ask why the boys kept throwing rocks around their tent all night, about 150 feet away.
They hadn't.
He still wonders if something out there in the dark was copying them.

Summer of 2003, high in the Ansel Adams Wilderness, a guy fresh out of college and a friend are on the last night of their first real backcountry trip, camped beside Garnet Lake next to a little snowmelt pond with a cliff on the far side. Every night they've hung their food bag, a blue mesh laundry bag on a long rope, out over that cliff edge, with the rope tied off to a tree up top.

On the last night, for reasons neither of them remembers, they leave the bear canisters on the ground away from the tent and only hang their day packs of snacks in the blue bag. Chewy fruit candies in individual wrappers, and mini beef jerky sticks in sealed plastic.
Around one or two in the morning they wake up to noises outside, a big animal, or several, moving around camp. Bears, they figure, batting at the canisters.
Then something brushes the tent right beside his friend's head.
His friend grabs a little pocket knife and wants to go out and look, and he talks him out of it, and eventually they both fall back asleep.

In the morning the blue bag isn't hanging from the cliff anymore. They climb around to the top and find it lying beside the tree with a hole torn in the bottom. The day packs have been pulled out and ripped open, and the rope is neatly piled beside them.

Every snack has been eaten, and what's left is sorted into two separate piles. One is the candy wrappers, each one unwrapped, not torn. The other is the jerky wrappers, each one sliced open with a single straight cut down the middle. The deodorant and toiletries haven't been touched.
For years he told it as a funny bear story. Now he's not so sure.

Pulling a rope up hand over hand leaves a pile, but a bear dragging it would back away and leave it strung out in a long line. Opening those candies takes two hands and a fingernail. Slicing a little jerky packet that cleanly takes one hand to hold it and another to cut. A bear, he figures, would've just eaten them wrapper and all.
Whatever was in their camp that night, it left everything in tidy order.

He's sixteen, backpacking with three friends deep in the Huron-Manistee National Forest in Michigan, and they've camped on a ridge above the river. At sunset, from the opposite ridge, comes a sound like a really strong man chopping firewood in perfect rhythm, way out in steep country where nobody should be chopping anything.

On the second night a distant pack of coyotes starts yipping, and then something answers from about a mile off, a long wail, like they're talking to each other. Later he wakes to that same scream from right across the river, so loud he feels it in his bones. Then the chopping starts again, heavy blows on wood from all around them, and from above, maybe ten feet over their heads. He lies frozen until dawn, and in the morning they get out.
A year later he hears recordings of supposed Sasquatch calls and wood knocks, and they match exactly. So he talks one friend into going back to the same spot, with a camera and plenty of guns.

After dark they crouch in the moonlight watching a hollow inside a huge fallen tree by the river, and his friend raises his rifle with shaking hands and whispers that he can see something moving. Then the friend turns and sprints for camp.
He follows, sweeping his spotlight across the ferns, and catches a big brownish blur keeping pace with them about thirty feet away, darting between the trees.

They zip themselves into the tent and wait. From out where it went comes a soft, curious cooing, like a primate, and it's getting closer. Then quiet, rhythmic footsteps on two legs, right beside the tent.
Through the nylon, he watches the shape of what looks like a hand reach toward his friend's head, and slowly feel the top of it from outside, almost stroking it.

His friend lies there with his pistol pointed at it, tears running down his face, paralyzed. And he finds himself laughing, helplessly, at the two of them lying there with their high-powered rifles. "We were completely powerless." He can't make himself look up through the mesh.
Finally it stops, and they hear big branches snapping as something large moves off.
At first light they find a young tree, thick as an ankle, snapped in half at chest height. It wasn't broken the day before.

It's a birthday party in the Mount Hood National Forest, about an hour from Salem, Oregon, a dozen friends swimming and drinking down by a river at a spot so remote you can only find it with directions like turn right at the tree with a 5 spray-painted on it. Nobody else around for miles. The cars are parked at the top of a really steep hill above the camp.

He's an Eagle Scout who's done week-long survival trips and had more run-ins with bears than he'd like, and he's a skeptic who's never once met a ghost. He's given some friends driving up from New Jersey those same hopeless directions, but with no signal and dark coming down, he doesn't expect them to find it.
Around midnight he thinks he hears somebody moving around up by the cars. Maybe his friends made it after all, so he leaves the fire and heads for the hill.
He's right at the bottom of the slope when it rings out. Whhhh-OOP. Whhhhhhh-OOP.
In all his years in the woods he's never heard anything like it.

He runs up that hill, a good thirty seconds of climbing, and gets to the top just as his friends' headlights come over the rise. Before he can even ask how they found the place he blurts out, Was that you? They have no idea what he's talking about. They've been driving, and they haven't heard a thing.
And then, in that confused silence, there are two knocks, like a rock hitting a tree.
A few seconds later comes the loudest crack he's ever heard in the woods, like somebody snapped a hundred-year-old oak right in half.
Then nothing.

Back down at the fire, everybody heard the whoop and the crash, and they all figured he'd made them himself. Years later he was watching a TV show when they played what researchers think a Sasquatch call sounds like, a long whoop, and he knew it the second he heard it.

Northern Minnesota, a summer night in 2014. He lives in a one-storey house on an acre and a half, with hundreds of acres of state forest behind it, and he's been a serious outdoorsman his whole life. He knows wolves and coyotes. He's hunted black bears, and once came nose to nose with one at its den, and all it did was snap its jaws at him. Black bears don't growl.

Around eleven he's watching TV when he remembers he's left the sprinkler running. So he goes out the back door, across the deck and down three steps into the dark yard, and turns toward the outdoor tap at the corner of the house.
As he steps off the deck, he hears a growl.

It's long and low, coming from behind a bush at the corner of the house, about fifteen feet from him and about five feet from the tap. It isn't especially loud, but it's deep, very deep and guttural, the sound of something with big lungs and a big throat, and it's unlike any animal he's ever heard.

Normally he'd freeze, or run, or at least look. Instead this strange, total calm comes over him. Not euphoria, just a deep sense of peace. And he actually says out loud, "Oh, stop growling, I'm just going to shut the water off."
He keeps walking until he's about five feet from that growl. He turns off the tap. He turns his back on it, and strolls inside to his easy chair, and he never even looks.
About half an hour later the numbness wears off, and it hits him. What on earth was that, and what did he just do? He goes back out on the deck and there's nothing.
That calm is nothing like him. Not long after, he stepped out on that same deck after dark, a deer snorted somewhere nearby, and he ran inside like a little kid.

He's wondered since if whatever was behind that bush somehow made him feel safe, like it was telling him it meant no harm. And the growl, he figures, was just what a big animal sounds like when it's saying that's close enough.

October, the Meherrin River in southern Virginia, a small river that's hard to get to, and he's taking three buddies on his first overnight trip down it. They put in after dark, after waiting on one guy to get off work, and find their way three hours downstream by flashlight to a sandbar he knows, the only spot with easy access to the woods for firewood.
They send one guy up the wooded slope above the sandbar to gather wood. It's about two hundred yards to the top, and they stand there watching his cheap flashlight bob up the hill.
Then they hear a scream.

The light comes back down the hill, fast. He falls a few times, his flashlight dies halfway, and somehow he makes it back to the sandbar without running into a tree. All he'll say is that something big got up right in front of him, and it wasn't a deer, and it wasn't a bear.

After that they arm up and grab whatever wood they can find along the bank instead. They've left the tent back at the put-in, of course, so three of them dig their sleeping bags into the sand around the fire, and the fourth insists on standing watch with a borrowed rifle and a box of rounds. By about four in the morning the fire, the last flashlight and all four of them are out cold.
They wake up with the sun melting the frost off their sleeping bags.

The boats are anchored at the bottom end of the sandbar, in a little pool beside the woods. Just outside camp there's a tree about six inches thick at the base, and about six feet up it's been twisted, shredded and folded over. The rest of the trunk, about twenty feet of it, has been rammed down the bank and into one of their boats.
The boat is half sunk.
They took it as a warning, waded out, freed the boat and got out of there as fast as they could. He's the only one of the four who still paddles that river, and he hasn't camped on it since.

He was a logger on the west coast of British Columbia in the 1950s, a bush boss who went on to become a chief forester, and his family says he was stoic and rational and hard to spook. He only talked about these things a handful of times. But he once told his grandkid that sometimes you're just not meant to have answers.

In 1951, at a logging camp, he watches from about a hundred metres away as a big, black-haired figure walks the length of the camp on two legs. It's as tall as the cookhouse eaves, about nine feet. The crew has stacked full drums of diesel against the cookhouse doors, several hundred pounds apiece, and it picks up each one and tosses it aside like an empty box, tears the doors off their hinges and ducks inside. Twenty minutes later it rushes out into the bush, and the meat locker has been ripped open and the ham half eaten. The company moves the whole camp ten miles.

In 1954 he's walking a ridge with a small crew, laying out a new road with survey stakes, when he spots what looks like a huge bear at the river's edge below them. They heard loud whoops earlier and figured it was some kind of bird.
Then it stands up on two legs. It walks ten feet and lets out a long whooop, and then a deafening sound somewhere between a growl and a scream.
Three men drop their stakes and run. Another one freezes, white as a ghost, hugging a cedar, and the thing crashes off into the brush.

He grabs the frozen man by the collar, picks up a dropped axe and hurries down the trail toward the crew bus. And something keeps pace with them through the trees, on both sides. Whenever he stops to listen, it stops. The air fills with a musty, rotten stench.
On the road back to camp he picks up two of the men who ran. They quit that day, along with the man he dragged out, and they leave the coast.
The third man who ran, the family says, was never found, and they searched for two weeks.

He lives on the outskirts of town, five miles from the nearest gas station, forest all around and a single neighbour across the road. In 2013 he picks a bucket of squash from his garden, sets it on the porch and forgets about it overnight.

In the morning the whole bucket is gone. A raccoon would've rummaged around and spilled squash everywhere, but nothing's spilled. It's like something picked the bucket up and carefully carried it off.

A few days later he comes home from work to a dead mouse on his doorstep, carefully wrapped in a leaf with some grass, almost like a sandwich. He wonders if someone's pranking him, or even trying to put some kind of curse on him.
Then nothing, for about a year.

One evening, watching TV, he catches movement through the window by the garden. A figure is hunched over the squash plants. He goes out to confront it, and what gets him is how quietly it's moving, like it's trying not to be heard.
The porch boards creak under his foot. It looks up, and its eyes shine in the porch light.

Then it stands up on two legs. Big and bulky, at least seven feet tall, black and hairy and shaped like a man. The second it sees him it takes off into the woods, unbelievably fast and still barely making a sound.
He lies awake that night thinking about the missing bucket and the wrapped-up mouse.

So the next morning he tries an experiment. He rolls some turkey up in a leaf with some grass, the way the mouse was wrapped, and leaves it on the picnic table when he goes to work. That evening it's gone, leaf, grass and all, and the lawn around the table doesn't look disturbed. And on his doorstep there's another mouse, headless this time, with a little pile of berries beside it.

The exchange has kept going ever since. Not long ago he got a whole deer antler. He's set up trail cameras plenty of times and never caught a thing, and it feels like it's always watching, he says. It just stays away whenever the cameras are up.

He lives in a trailer at the top of a farm on the side of Mount Ida, out in the middle of nowhere in the BC Interior. No cell service, no neighbours within shouting distance, and forest on every side except the little road up. Since he was a kid he's heard stories about that mountain from the Indigenous people of the area, and the short version of all of them is that people stay off it.

It's a January night, around 10:45, and three sets of sirens go by on the road below. In fifteen years out there he's heard exactly one siren before, and that was earlier the same week. Half an hour later the power goes out. He's already in bed in the dark, and he only notices because the wifi drops.
Out there, no wifi means you're completely on your own.

Then, out of nowhere, there's a sharp, loud cry, like a little kid who's just wiped out on a bike, and then hysterical crying. His dogs go nuts at the door. He's heard plenty of cougars, and they can mimic a crying child scarily well, so he lies there telling himself that's all it is. Honestly, a cougar is the best-case scenario.
The dogs finally settle down, and he's trying to get some sleep, when the second sound comes.

He's never heard anything like it. Five seconds of pure screeching, like every horror movie monster at once, "a demonic banshee with the vocal cords of a T. rex." The bass in it shakes his bed. It's like somebody hid a concert sound system out there in the forest.

Now the dogs are snarling and growling at the door like whatever screamed is right on the other side. He can taste his heartbeat. His generator and his router are both up in the barn, out there in the dark, and he isn't going anywhere, so he lies in bed checking his phone every thirty seconds for wifi until he finally falls asleep.

In the morning everything's back to normal. The sirens and the outage were a car hitting a power pole a kilometre down the road. He checks around the yard, and there are no tracks. Nobody in the local Facebook group heard a thing.
The first cry, he's happy to call a cougar. The second one, he just can't.

This is about a grandfather who went into the woods of the BC coast as a boy in the 1940s, worked the tugs and the log booms, built logging roads, and was a foreman and bush boss by 1955. His family says he was stoic and practical, and he told almost nobody what he saw out there. He saw it three times.

The first time was 1951. From about a hundred metres away he watched a huge, black-haired figure walk right across a logging camp to the cookhouse, its head level with the roof, nearly nine feet tall. Over weekends the crews stacked full diesel barrels against the cookhouse doors. It tossed them aside one by one, tore the doors off their hinges, ducked inside, and stayed in there about twenty minutes before it rushed out into the bush.
The lard, the butter, the sugar and the honey were all gone, the meat locker was ripped open, and there was a ham half eaten. They moved the whole camp ten miles.

In 1954 he and a small crew were staking out a road along a ridge above a river when what he took for a big bear down at the water stood up on two legs. It walked about ten feet, gave a loud whoop, and then a deafening holler, somewhere between a growl and a scream. Three of the men dropped their stakes and ran.

He grabbed a man frozen stiff against a cedar, picked up a dropped axe and headed for the crew bus. And the whole way, something heavy moved through the trees on both sides of them, stopping whenever he stopped, while a musty, rotten smell kept getting stronger until it was sickening.
Two of the men who ran got picked up on the road. The way the family tells it, the third was never found.

The last time was near Pemberton in 1962. He was walking his bulldozer back to the fuel trailer at dusk when one at least eight feet tall crossed the road a hundred feet ahead of him in two strides. It looked at him, and its eyes glowed orange-red in the machine's lights.
Then it crashed off into the forest, and he watched trees twenty-five and thirty feet tall sway like grass as it went.
By then he knew exactly what it was. He finished that road over the next two weeks and never saw it again.
Atlin, British Columbia, sometime in the early 2000s. It's a tiny town on Atlin Lake just south of the Yukon border, with nothing but wilderness all the way around it.

Our witness grew up in the Yukon and spent years on hunting trips in the bush, and has come up from southern BC with a girlfriend to visit family in Whitehorse. Today the two of them are on a day trip, and after a soak in some little warm springs off an old mining road, they drive on further and find a spur road that ends at a pullout where hunters unload their ATVs.
There's a narrow trail climbing off through the forest up the mountain, so they head up it to stretch their legs. They haven't seen another person or another vehicle all day.
The usual birds and squirrels are calling in the trees around them.
And then the whole forest goes completely silent.
Not a bird. Not a squirrel. Nothing.

A few moments later the silence is split wide open by the loudest, most aggressive scream either of them has ever heard. It sounds like an animal, but it also sounds way too human, like somebody shrieking with rage at the top of their lungs.

They look at each other, and they turn around and walk as fast as they can back down to the vehicle, and once they're inside, they sit there watching the trees for a minute, to see if anything followed them down.
Nothing comes out. They drive away shaking.
There are no cougars that far north. And a lifelong Yukon hunter knows exactly what a bear sounds like.
Whatever screamed up on that trail, it wasn't either one.
